How Does Urban Green Data Center Policy Empower 
Corporate Energy Utilization Efficiency? Evidence from 
China 
    
Against the backdrop of China’s “dual-carbon” goals and the deepening national digital 
transformation strategy, urban green data center development has emerged as a key policy 
instrument for improving firms’ energy utilization efficiency and advancing the green and low-
carbon transition. Drawing on unbalanced firm-year panel that links Chinese A-share listed firms to 
prefecture-level cities from 2012 to 2024, this study employs a staggered-adoption difference-in-
differences (DID) framework to systematically estimate the effect of urban green data center policy 
on corporate energy utilization efficiency and to clarify the mechanisms at play. The results show 
that the policy significantly enhances firms’ energy utilization efficiency. Mechanism tests suggest 
that the effect operates primarily through two channels: improved ESG performance and policy-
induced increases in firms’ green investment. Heterogeneity analyses indicate that the policy impact 
is stronger in resource-based cities, in more competitive industries, and among mature-stage firms. 
Moderation analyses further show that executives’ green cognition significantly strengthens the 
policy’s marginal effect on energy utilization efficiency. By contrast, executives’ digital cognition 
tends to weaken the policy effect when considered alone; however, when executives simultaneously 
exhibit high levels of both green and digital cognition, their synergistic alignment yields a 
significantly positive enabling effect. Specifically, an integrated cognitive profile helps alleviate the 
adjustment costs of early-stage digital transformation and fosters integrated innovation between 
green and digital technologies, thereby further reinforcing the policy’s enabling role. In addition, as 
successive pilot batches expand, the policy’s diffusion effect exhibits a nonlinear trajectory, 
increasing initially and then declining thereafter. Building on these findings, this study derives 
policy implications and provides China-specific empirical evidence and managerial insights for 
developing countries seeking to achieve energy transition and sustainable development while 
unlocking digital dividends. 
 
Keywords: green data center policy; corporate energy utilization efficiency; executive green 
cognition; executive digital cognition 
 
1. Introduction and Literature Review 
Against the backdrop of intensifying global climate change and the accelerating energy 
transition, improving energy utilization efficiency is not only a critical pathway for China to advance 
green and low-carbon development and achieve its carbon peaking and carbon neutrality (“dual-
carbon”) goals, but also a core driver for alleviating resource and environmental constraints, shaping 
new development advantages, and steering the greening transformation of future industries. More 
importantly, for developing countries, where industrialization and urbanization continue to advance, 
energy demand remains rigidly growing, and fiscal and technological constraints are often more 
binding, enhancing energy utilization efficiency is both a feasible approach to jointly promoting 
economic growth and achieving energy conservation and carbon mitigation at lower cost, and a 

strategic lever, as well as an urgent task, for strengthening energy security and resilience, improving 
international competitiveness, and advancing sustainable development. The white paper China’s 
Energy Transition explicitly calls for “unswervingly accelerating the energy transition” and 
“continuously improving energy utilization efficiency.” As major actors in energy consumption and 
carbon emissions, firms’ energy utilization efficiency directly shapes the overall decarbonization 
trajectory and the landscape of green competitiveness. Accordingly, improving corporate energy 
utilization efficiency has become a key focal point for advancing the energy transition and high-
quality development. Yet, progress in improving corporate energy utilization efficiency still faces 
prominent real-world constraints and implementation bottlenecks. On the one hand, many firms 
remain weak in foundational capabilities such as data collection, governance, and application, 
making it difficult to achieve fine-grained monitoring, diagnosis, and optimization of energy 
consumption processes. On the other hand, insufficient managerial cognition and organizational 
capacity in green transformation and digital governance often prevents energy-saving and 
emissions-reduction goals from being effectively embedded into strategic decision-making and day-
to-day operations, thereby undermining the persistence and replicability of efficiency improvements  
(Geng et al., 2024). Under these “dual constraints,” it is challenging for firms to realize systematic 
gains in energy utilization efficiency, underscoring the need for coordinated advances in process-
wide technological innovation and managerial innovation to translate energy saving and efficiency 
enhancement into substantive improvements in green competitiveness. 
Although conventional policies such as the Low-Carbon City pilots and the Broadband China 
pilots have achieved notable progress in guiding regional green transition and strengthening the 
digital infrastructure foundation, respectively, their policy objectives and mechanisms are relatively 
fragmented and tend to emphasize a single dimension. As a result, they are less able to generate 
synergy within an integrated framework that jointly advances green governance and digital 
empowerment, and thus may struggle to systematically overcome key bottlenecks in energy-
intensive sectors’ efficiency improvement and low-carbon transition. By contrast, the green data 
center policy organically integrates green and low-carbon principles with the upgrading of digital 
infrastructure. It not only emphasizes energy efficiency enhancement and carbon emissions control, 
but also leverages advanced digital technologies to strengthen firms’ data foundations. By targeting 
data centers as a critical hub, this policy provides a synergistic, empowerment-oriented pathway that 
combines a clear green objective with robust support for digital capabilities, thereby facilitating 
improvements in corporate energy utilization efficiency. Since the 13th Five-Year Plan period, with 
the successive promulgation and implementation of policy documents such as the Guiding Opinions 
on Strengthening Green Data Center Development and the mandatory national standard Data Center 
Energy Efficiency Limits and Energy Efficiency Grades, energy-efficiency thresholds and grading 
requirements for data centers have been clearly specified and gradually tightened. These measures 
have accelerated the greening upgrade of green data centers as a key component of digital 
infrastructure and have, from the supply side, provided firms with more efficient and cleaner green 
computing power. Meanwhile, relevant authorities have organized an annual recommendation and 
selection program for “National Green Data Centers,” using criteria such as a power usage 
effectiveness (PUE) threshold of 1.30 or below as a core entry threshold and establishing industry 
benchmarks for energy efficiency. This initiative not only strengthens policy signals and market 
expectations regarding efficiency improvement, but also offers firms an operational and official 
reference through a quantifiable and comparable evaluation system, thereby enabling them to 

optimize energy-efficiency governance and benchmark against best practices. At a critical stage 
when China is accelerating efforts to improve energy utilization efficiency and advance the green 
and low-carbon transition, how to leverage the institutional supply and incentive mechanisms 
embedded in the green data center policy to systematically enhance firms’ digital capabilities and 
energy management, and thereby overcome technical and governance bottlenecks in efficiency 
improvement, has become a frontier issue for supporting high-quality development. More broadly, 
the policy practice surrounding green data centers can also provide a transferable pathway for 
developing countries. That is, while advancing digital transformation, countries can simultaneously 
strengthen the orientation toward green development, prompting green governance to shift from ex 
post remediation to upstream embedding and thereby weakening the conventional path dependence 
of “pollute first, treat later.” At the same time, by balancing energy security and economic growth, 
they can jointly enhance digital competitiveness and low-carbon transition capacity, and thus 
achieve sustainable development goals in a more robust manner. 
The literature related to this study can be broadly categorized into two strands. The first strand 
focuses on identifying the determinants of improvements in corporate energy utilization efficiency. 
At the micro level, existing studies generally argue that internal firm characteristics, including firm 
size, ownership structure (Chen and Chen, 2019), export status (Yang, 2023), technological 
innovation capability (Lu and Li, 2024), and the level of digitalization (Wang et al., 2025), are key 
drivers of higher energy utilization efficiency. At the macro and meso levels, some scholars further 
suggest that external environmental factors, such as regional economic development (Fang, 2023), 
industrial agglomeration (Wang et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2024), and the degree of market integration  
(Song et al., 2025), also exert significant positive effects on corporate energy utilization efficiency. 
In addition, a growing body of research adopts the perspective of policy intervention to examine the 
enabling effects of single environmental or financial policies, providing broadly consistent evidence 
across environmental regulation policies such as carbon emissions trading (Zhang and Cai, 2022), 
pollutant discharge permit trading (Lin and Dong, 2021), differential electricity pricing (Chen et al., 
2025), and low-carbon city pilots (Song and Jin, 2025), as well as financial-policy instruments such 
as tax policies (Zwick and Mahon, 2017; Xu and Zwick, 2024). The second strand examines the 
implementation effects of the green data center policy. Existing research on this policy has primarily 
verified its positive role in promoting sustainable development from perspectives such as green 
innovation leadership (Han et al., 2025; Li and Yang, 2023), the agglomeration of resources and 
production factors (Xiong et al., 2025), and carbon emissions reduction (Ji et al., 2025; Li et al., 
2023). However, a salient limitation remains. Most studies adopt a fragmented approach that 
evaluates the effects of either greening policies or digitalization policies on corporate energy 
utilization efficiency in isolation, while offering limited systematic discussion of the synergistic 
mechanisms generated by deep green-digital integration. In particular, under the green data center 
policy, a typical context of green-digital integration, its potential influence on corporate energy 
utilization efficiency has not yet received sufficient systematic attention or rigorous empirical 
testing. 
Addressing these gaps, this study draws on matched data for Chinese A-share listed firms and 
prefecture-level cities from 2012 to 2024 and employs a staggered-adoption difference-in-
differences (DID) framework to systematically evaluate the impact of the green data center policy 
on corporate energy utilization efficiency, while further identifying the underlying mechanisms and 
heterogeneous effects. Relative to the existing literature, the marginal contributions of this study are 

threefold. First, it moves beyond the conventional analytical framework that treats digitalization and 
greening policies as separate domains by focusing on the green data center policy as an institutional 
vehicle for green-digital integration, thereby revealing its synergistic pathway for enhancing 
corporate energy utilization efficiency. Second, grounded in upper echelons theory, it introduces 
executives’ green cognition and executives’ digital cognition as key moderating factors and 
systematically tests their moderating effects and synergistic mechanisms in the policy transmission 
process. In doing so, it shows that policy effectiveness depends to a large extent on the degree of 
alignment between executives’ green and digital cognition, offering empirical insights for firms 
seeking to improve strategic cognitive fit and fully capture policy dividends. Third, adopting a 
macro-meso-micro analytical lens, and integrating resource endowment theory, industrial 
organization theory, and corporate life-cycle theory, it examines how policy effects vary across 
different resource endowment types, market structure characteristics, and life-cycle stages, thereby 
extending a context-sensitive theoretical framework for analyzing the green data center policy. 
Overall, this study not only deepens our understanding of the contexts and transmission logic 
through which the green data center policy operates, but also provides more context-adaptive 
theoretical foundations and practical reference for governments to optimize differentiated policy 
design and for firms to advance energy-efficiency improvement in light of their specific conditions. 
2. Theoretical Analysis and Research Hypotheses 
By promoting the greening upgrade of digital infrastructure, the green data center policy 
provides an important external institutional condition for improving corporate energy utilization 
efficiency. As critical infrastructure underpinning the operation of the digital economy, 
improvements in the energy efficiency of green data centers are not confined to their own 
operational sphere. Rather, through technological spillovers and diffusion effects, such 
improvements are gradually transmitted to firms’ production and operational processes, thereby 
exerting a systematic influence on corporate energy utilization efficiency. In the construction and 
operation of green data centers, high-efficiency computing equipment and intelligent energy 
management technologies are increasingly integrated. By raising energy performance, these 
upgrades reduce firms’ data-storage and computing costs structurally and, through cloud access and 
computing services, encourage the adoption of energy-saving technologies (Xiong et al., 2025). 
When firms substitute green computing power for traditional self-built or inefficient IT resources, 
they effectively reduce the energy input required per unit of computing power at a given scale of 
production, thus improving the alignment between energy inputs and outputs. These supply-side 
upgrades generate technological spillovers that provide stable and low-cost external support for 
improving corporate energy utilization efficiency. Meanwhile, by establishing energy-efficiency 
standards and demonstration benchmarks, the green data center policy creates normative 
institutional pressure that facilitates the diffusion of green management principles across firms (Luo 
et al., 2025). A unified energy-efficiency evaluation system provides firms with clear benchmarking 
references, alleviating information asymmetry and uncertainty about transition pathways during 
energy-saving transformation. This, in turn, encourages firms to adjust their energy structure 
through imitative learning and managerial optimization, thereby improving energy utilization 
efficiency. Under the combined pressure of industry competition and external assessments, firms 
increasingly embed energy constraints into production organization and operational decision-
making, promoting a shift in energy management from extensive input expansion to more refined 
governance. As a result, the green data center policy not only directly reduces firms’ energy intensity 

through technological spillovers, but also reinforces sustained improvements in energy utilization 
efficiency through the diffusion of managerial paradigms. Based on the above reasoning, this study 
proposes the following hypotheses: 
H1: The green data center policy significantly promotes corporate energy utilization efficiency. 
Although the green data center policy provides firms with strong external institutional 
incentives and technological infrastructure support, whether these policy dividends can be 
effectively translated into internal improvements in energy utilization efficiency depends largely on 
firms’ strategic responsiveness. Grounded in upper echelons theory, corporate decisions are driven 
by executives with specific backgrounds, experiences, values, and cognitive structures. As the core 
decision-makers shaping corporate strategy (Wang and Li, 2017), top managers’ dual cognition of 
the green development orientation and the digital enablement pathway embedded in the green data 
center policy will influence firms’ strategic choices regarding energy-efficiency investment and 
technological upgrading, thereby shaping both the trajectory and the realized outcomes of 
improvements in energy utilization efficiency. Executive green cognition refers to the cognitive and 
knowledge structure formed by executives on the basis of their understanding of resource and 
environmental issues and their psychological experiences in fulfilling responsibilities for resource 
conservation and environmental protection (Wu et al., 2024). It constitutes a psychological 
foundation for corporate green strategic decision-making (Zou et al., 2019). Specifically, executive 
teams with strong green cognition are more likely to perceive the positive signals conveyed by the 
green data center policy and to recognize that improving energy efficiency is not merely a 
compliance requirement, but also a strategic opportunity to build long-term green competitive 
advantage (He et al., 2013). Accordingly, they tend to view the policy as a catalyst for internal green 
transformation, and thus allocate resources more proactively, optimize production processes, adopt 
energy-saving innovative technologies (Liang et al., 2022), and establish robust energy management 
systems to maximize the policy dividends. In this context, the positive effect of the green data center 
policy on corporate energy utilization efficiency is expected to be substantially amplified. By 
contrast, when executives exhibit low levels of green cognition, their attention to environmental 
issues, understanding of sustainability strategies, and assessment of the value of green policies are 
all likely to be limited. Under such circumstances, even if a firm is covered by the green data center 
policy, the executive team may fail to fully identify the energy-efficiency opportunities embedded 
in the policy. They may instead interpret the policy primarily as an external compliance burden or a 
change in technological infrastructure, rather than strategically linking it to core objectives such as 
optimizing energy management and improving operational efficiency. This deficiency in green 
cognition weakens firms’ intrinsic motivation and capability to proactively connect with, deeply 
integrate, and effectively utilize green data center resources, thereby preventing policy dividends 
from being transmitted to corporate energy-related practices. Based on the above reasoning, this 
study proposes the following hypothesis: 
H2: Executive green cognition strengthens the effect of the green data center policy on 
corporate energy utilization efficiency. 
Executives’ digital cognition captures the extent to which the top management team 
understands and applies digital technologies and recognizes their potential to drive business 
transformation (Yu et al., 2024). The green data center policy is designed to deliver computing 
services in a more centralized, efficient, and environmentally friendly manner by upgrading digital 
infrastructure. Whether firms can effectively capitalize on this external enablement therefore 

depends critically on their internal capacity to absorb and convert digital resources. Specifically, 
executive teams with strong digital cognition can clearly identify the core value provided by green 
data centers, including data-driven capabilities and intelligent operations and maintenance (Ma et 
al., 2025). They are not only able to connect to and integrate high-efficiency external computing 
resources, but also able to use these resources to build internal digital energy management systems 
that enable real-time monitoring, accurate diagnosis, and intelligent optimization of energy 
consumption. This inside and outside linkage in digital capability allows firms to embed the 
advantages of the green data center policy seamlessly into their energy management practices, 
thereby substantially amplifying the policy’s positive effect on energy-efficiency improvement. 
Importantly, the moderating role of executive digital cognition is not uniformly positive. On the one 
hand, if executives lack adequate digital cognition, firms may face a situation in which resources 
are available but cannot be effectively utilized, even when they fall within the policy coverage of 
green data centers. Executives may view the data center merely as a basic IT outsourcing service 
and fail to understand the underlying logic of energy-efficiency optimization and the value of data. 
As a consequence, firms may miss opportunities to adopt advanced digital tools for refined energy 
management, causing the policy effect of green data centers to become largely symbolic and 
substantially weakened. In this case, insufficient executive digital cognition constrains the 
realization of policy effectiveness. 
On the other hand, although executive digital cognition generally helps firms seize 
opportunities associated with the green data center policy, excessively high digital cognition may 
also produce unintended adverse effects. Executive teams with strong digital cognition often show 
pronounced strategic enthusiasm for digital technologies and tend to interpret the green data center 
policy primarily as an opportunity to accelerate digital transformation (Fan and Yan, 2025). 
However, without alignment with green principles, this digital-cognition advantage may translate 
into an impulse toward computing capacity expansion. Firms may overemphasize investments in 
computing power to capture markets and scale operations, while paying comparatively less attention 
to improving energy efficiency through key energy-saving technologies and process reengineering 
(Ma and Wei, 2025). This bias toward prioritizing digital expansion over energy saving can also 
lead to resource misallocation in the policy response. Even if operational efficiency improves at the 
data-center level, a firm’s overall energy consumption may still increase markedly. If energy inputs 
driven by digital expansion grow faster than operating revenue, the economic value created per unit 
of energy input will decline, generating a computing rebound effect (Li, 2025). Therefore, when 
executive digital cognition is strong but not coordinated with green cognition, the firm’s response 
to the green data center policy may shift from an enabling tool to an energy-consumption driver, 
thereby weakening the policy’s positive effect on corporate energy utilization efficiency. Based on 
the above reasoning, this study proposes the following hypotheses: 
H3a: Executive digital cognition strengthens the effect of the green data center policy on 
corporate energy utilization efficiency. 
H3b: Executive digital cognition weakens the effect of the green data center policy on corporate 
energy utilization efficiency. 
Senior executives’ green cognition and digital cognitive capability are not isolated attributes; 
instead, they exhibit strong strategic complementarity. The former provides a value orientation and 
internal motivation for enhancing corporate energy efficiency, addressing why energy efficiency 
should be improved. The latter offers technological enablement and implementation pathways, 

addressing how energy efficiency can be improved effectively. Together, they constitute a dual 
strategic engine that empowers firms’ low carbon digital transformation (Wang et al., 2025). 
Specifically, the synergy between executives’ green cognition and digital cognition can strengthen 
the effect of green data center policies on firms’ energy utilization efficiency through a closed loop 
mechanism consisting of goal alignment, resource allocation, organizational implementation, and 
continuous improvement. At the goal level, stronger green cognition encourages managers to 
interpret the policy as a comprehensive signal that combines energy efficiency discipline with the 
cultivation of green competitive advantage. Accordingly, firms embed energy efficiency objectives 
into strategic planning, key performance indicators, and performance appraisal systems, thereby 
avoiding an implementation bias that prioritizes digitalization while neglecting energy saving. At 
the resource allocation level, green cognition increases the priority of investments in energy saving 
retrofits, energy efficiency management systems, and green process upgrading, whereas digital 
cognition enhances the allocation efficiency of data resources, algorithmic tools, intelligent 
equipment, and platform-based systems. Their coupling redirects investment away from capacity 
stacking toward energy-efficiency-oriented digital investment, reducing energy consumption per 
unit of output through structural optimization of capital expenditures and operating expenditures. 
At the organizational implementation level, green cognition strengthens executives’ capacity to 
mobilize cross functional collaboration for energy governance, enabling coordinated action across 
production, equipment, information technology, finance, and ESG related functions. Digital 
cognition supports the construction of a digital management chain covering energy metering, data 
collection, process diagnostics, strategy optimization, and performance evaluation, allowing 
external policy momentum to be translated more smoothly into actionable internal rules for energy 
management. At the continuous improvement level, the long-term commitment and risk discipline 
fostered by green cognition, combined with the data feedback, algorithm iteration, and 
organizational learning enabled by digital cognition, facilitate an iterative mechanism of energy 
efficiency improvement, feedback calibration, process optimization, and renewed improvement. 
This mechanism transforms the policy shock from a one time improvement into a sustainable 
capability for energy efficiency governance. Therefore, when executive teams possess both strong 
green cognition and strong digital cognitive capability, they are more likely to form a dual drive 
configuration in which green orientation and digital capability jointly reinforce each other. 
Strategically, they fully acknowledge the value of energy efficiency enhancement; operationally, 
they effectively deploy digital tools to achieve energy saving and efficiency gains. As a result, they 
can more fully unlock the positive role of green data center policies in promoting corporate energy 
utilization efficiency and convert external policy momentum into internal impetus for energy 
management (Xiong et al., 2025). Based on the above reasoning, this study proposes the following 
hypotheses: 
H4: The synergy between senior executives’ green cognition and digital cognitive capability 
strengthens the impact of green data center policies on firms’ energy utilization efficiency.

3. Research Design 
3.1. Variable Definitions 
3.1.1. Dependent Variable: Corporate Energy Utilization Efficiency (Ee) 
The dependent variable in this study is corporate energy utilization efficiency. Following prior 
studies (Liu et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2022), we use the natural logarithm of the ratio of operating 
revenue to a firm’s total energy consumption as a proxy for corporate energy utilization efficiency. 
A higher value indicates greater economic value created per unit of energy input, and therefore 
higher energy utilization efficiency. The construction procedure is as follows. First, we conduct data 
mining on each listed firm’s energy consumption information by extracting energy-related 
disclosures from annual reports, corporate social responsibility reports, and investor relations 
activity records. With authorization from local environmental authorities, we combine these 
disclosures with micro-level energy consumption databases maintained by the environmental 
agencies in the locations of the firm and its subsidiaries, and then compile firm-level annual energy 
consumption data. Second, using the standard coal conversion coefficients released by the National 
Energy Administration, we convert multiple types of energy consumption, including water use, 
electricity use, coal, natural gas, gasoline, diesel, and district heating, into a unified standard coal 
equivalent to obtain total energy consumption. Finally, we calculate the ratio of operating revenue 
to total energy consumption and take its natural logarithm to construct the indicator of corporate 
energy utilization efficiency. 
3.1.2. Core Explanatory Variable: Green Data Center Policy (Did) 
As a key information infrastructure supporting the coordinated development of China’s dual-
carbon strategy and the digital economy, green data centers aim to achieve a sustainable model 
through a combination of measures, including technological innovation, energy-efficiency target 
setting, life-cycle regulation and evaluation, and policy incentives, thereby improving energy 
efficiency, reducing environmental impacts, and promoting resource circularity. Regarding spatial 
deployment and industry selection, China emphasizes both regional coordination and sector 

representativeness. The policy prioritizes locations with national computing power hub nodes to 
leverage geographic and energy advantages, and it focuses on energy-intensive sectors such as 
manufacturing, telecommunications, and finance, with the objective of developing replicable 
pathways for green transformation. Following the approach of Li et al. (2025), we evaluate the 
micro-level effects of this policy using a staggered-adoption difference-in-differences design. 
Specifically, we construct the core explanatory variable Did as the interaction between a pilot-city 
indicator, which equals 1 for cities approved as pilots and 0 otherwise, and a post-policy indicator, 
which equals 1 for the pilot year and subsequent years and 0 otherwise. This specification enables 
us to identify the net policy effect of green data centers on corporate energy efficiency. 
3.1.3. Moderating Variables 
(1) Executive Green Cognition (Green_co) 
Following Li et al. (2023), we construct an index of executive green cognition based on three 
dimensions, namely cognition of green competitive advantage, cognition of corporate social 
responsibility, and perceived external environmental pressure. We select a set of keywords for each 
dimension and compute the ratio of the total frequency of these keywords appearing in annual report 
texts to the total number of words in the annual report. This index provides an objective measure of 
the attention allocation and cognitive orientation of the top management team toward green 
development. 
(2) Executive Digital Cognition (Dig_co) 
Following Qiao et al. (2025), we measure executive digital cognition using a hierarchical 
scoring scheme based on differences in executives’ organizational rank. The variable is coded as 1 
if at least one member of the top management team (TMT) has a digital background. It is coded as 
2 if the member with a digital background also serves on the board of directors. It is coded as 3 if 
the digital leader serves as the CEO or the chair of the board. If the firm has no executives with a 
digital background, the variable is coded as 0. A stronger structural power position within the 
executive team implies greater control and influence over the firm’s strategic decision-making 
process. 
3.1.4. Control Variables 
To ensure the robustness and reliability of the regression results, and following prior studies 
(Shi and Li, 2020; Yang and Cheng, 2019), we include control variables covering firm 
characteristics, financial conditions, and the macroeconomic environment. Specifically, the controls 
include economic development level (Pgdp, the natural logarithm of regional GDP per capita), 
industrial structure (Ind, the ratio of value added in the tertiary sector to regional GDP), government 
intervention (Gov, the ratio of local fiscal expenditure to regional GDP), firm age (Age, the natural 
logarithm of the difference between the current year and the firm’s founding year), loss status (Loss, 
which equals 1 if the previous year’s net profit is below zero and 0 otherwise), and firm value 
(Tobin’s Q). In addition, to mitigate endogeneity concerns arising from unobserved firm 
heterogeneity and time trends, we further incorporate multi-dimensional fixed effects at the firm 
and year levels, enabling identification of the causal effect of the green data center policy on 
corporate energy efficiency.

3.2.3 Sample Selection and Data Sources 
This study examines Chinese A-share listed firms over the period 2012 to 2024 and constructs 
an unbalanced firm-year panel dataset to evaluate the potential impact of the green data center policy 
on corporate energy efficiency. Firm-level data are primarily obtained from the CSMAR database 
and firms’ annual reports. City-level variables are compiled mainly from publicly available 
information released on the official website of the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology 
and from various editions of the China City Statistical Yearbook. To ensure sample 
representativeness and the validity of the empirical results, we screen the initial dataset using the 
following procedures. (1) We exclude firms in the financial and real estate industries to avoid 
distortions caused by industry-specific characteristics. (2) We remove firms labeled ST or PT to 
mitigate the influence of financially distressed firms. (3) To address missing data, we apply 
exponential smoothing for imputation. (4) To reduce potential biases caused by outliers, we 
winsorize all variables at the 1st and 99th percentiles. Descriptive statistics for the main variables 
are reported in Table 1.

4. Empirical Analysis 
4.1. Baseline Regression 
Following Model (1), we employ a stepwise regression approach to examine the effect of the 
green data center policy on corporate energy utilization efficiency. The baseline results are reported 
in Table 2. As shown in Column (1), the estimated coefficient on the core explanatory variable is 
significantly positive at the 1 percent level, providing initial evidence that the green data center 
policy exerts an enabling effect on corporate energy utilization efficiency. To further substantiate 
this finding, we progressively add control variables in Columns (2) to (7). The results indicate that 
although the positive coefficient on the green data center policy fluctuates slightly as additional 
controls are included, reflecting potential changes associated with omitted variables, it remains 
statistically significant at the 5 percent level or better throughout. This suggests that, after 
accounting for differences in regional economic conditions and firm-specific characteristics, the 
pilot policy continues to effectively improve corporate energy utilization efficiency, providing 
strong support for Hypothesis H1.

4.2. Robustness Checks 
4.2.1. Parallel Trends Test 
To validate the identification of the staggered-adoption difference-in-differences estimates, we 
conduct a parallel trends test using an event study specification to examine the dynamic evolution 
of the policy effect of the green data center pilots on corporate energy utilization efficiency. To 
mitigate multicollinearity, we collapse the sample accordingly. Figure 2 reports dynamic treatment 
effects for each period relative to the year before policy implementation, which serves as the 
baseline. The results show that, prior to policy implementation, the estimated coefficients for all 
leads fluctuate slightly around zero and their confidence intervals all include zero. This indicates 
that, before the pilot policy was introduced, there was no systematic difference in the trend of energy 
utilization efficiency between treated and control firms, consistent with the parallel trends 
assumption. After policy implementation, the estimated coefficients become significantly positive 
starting in the first year and increase over time, suggesting that the green data center policy produces 
a clear enabling effect on corporate energy utilization efficiency and that this effect is persistent and 
cumulative. The relatively limited effect in the early stage may reflect the phased and systemic 
nature of green data center development. Green data center construction is not an overnight endeavor. 
From the greening upgrade of computing infrastructure to the deep alignment of firms’ internal 
energy management systems, the process requires a construction cycle and technological absorption. 
As the pilot policy advances, policy dividends continue to be released through technological 
spillovers and managerial optimization, thereby driving sustained improvements in corporate energy 
utilization efficiency.

4.2.2. Placebo Test 
To rule out potential interference from omitted variables, random shocks, or other unobserved 
factors, we conduct a placebo test. Specifically, we randomly draw from the full sample a set of 
firms equal in size to the original treated group to form a pseudo treated group, and we randomly 
assign a policy implementation year to construct a fictitious policy shock term. We then repeat the 
random sampling and regression procedure 1,000 times and extract the pseudo estimated 
coefficients and corresponding p-values from each iteration. Figure 3 presents the kernel density 
distribution of the placebo coefficients along with a scatter plot of the associated p-values. The 
results show that the placebo coefficients generated by random simulation exhibit an approximately 
normal distribution, and the p-values in the vast majority of trials exceed 0.1 and fail to reach 
conventional significance levels, indicating that under random assignment the policy shock has no 
significant effect on energy utilization efficiency. In contrast, the actual coefficient from the baseline 
regression, equal to 0.0268, appears as a clear outlier away from zero and lies far outside the 
distribution of simulated coefficients. This evidence further suggests that the main findings are not 
driven by unobserved confounders and are therefore robust and credible.

4.2.3. Heckman Two-Step Procedure 
Because the spatial placement of green data center pilots is not fully random and instead 
depends heavily on pre-existing city-level data center scale and digital infrastructure endowments, 
this location-specific selection process may generate substantial self-selection bias and thereby 
distort the true policy effect. To address this concern, we apply the Heckman two-step procedure as 
a robustness check. In the first stage, we use the total volume of postal and telecommunications 
services in 1984, together with other control variables, as predictors of participation in the green 
data center policy. Based on these variables, we estimate a Probit model and compute the inverse 
Mills ratio (IMR), which is then included in the second-stage outcome regression. Because Probit 
models with fixed effects may suffer from estimation bias and high computational burden, we adopt 
the Mundlak correction by adding the firm-specific means of all time-varying explanatory and 
control variables to capture the correlation between unobserved heterogeneity and regressors. We 
also include a linear time trend to further enhance robustness. The Heckman estimates are reported 
in Column (1) of Table 4. The coefficient on the core explanatory variable remains significantly 
positive, consistent with the baseline results, while the IMR is not statistically significant. This 
suggests that sample selection has a limited influence on the estimates and that the baseline findings 
are not materially driven by self-selection bias. 
4.2.4. Bacon Decomposition 
In a staggered-adoption difference-in-differences setting, treatment timing differs across units. 
The traditional two-way fixed effects estimator can be expressed as a weighted average of all 
possible 2 by 2 difference-in-differences comparisons in the sample. When treatment effects are 
dynamically heterogeneous over time, comparisons between later treated units and earlier treated 
units can generate a “bad control group” problem, causing the baseline coefficient to deviate from 
the true effect. To diagnose and mitigate potential bias from such heterogeneous treatment effects, 
we apply the Bacon decomposition to examine the weights underlying the estimated average 
treatment effect of the green data center policy. As shown in Table 3 and Figure 4, there are 
substantial differences in the weight distribution across comparison types. Comparisons between 
the treated group and the never treated group account for the dominant share of the overall weight, 
reaching 75.5 percent, with an associated estimate of 0.061. Because this comparison does not 

involve differences in treatment timing, it is not affected by time-related heterogeneity in treatment 
effects. This indicates that the main estimated effect primarily reflects differences between pilot 
cities and control cities that were never included in the pilot program. Among comparisons involving 
treatment timing, the weight for comparisons between earlier treated and later treated groups is 15.1 
percent, with an estimated value of 0.025. The comparison most likely to introduce bias, namely 
later treated versus earlier treated groups, carries only 9.3 percent of the total weight and yields an 
estimate close to zero. Overall, although the sample does include cross comparisons among pilot 
cities approved in different years, the corresponding weights are limited and their influence on the 
overall estimate is small, suggesting that they are unlikely to materially affect the baseline 
conclusions.

4.3. Moderating Effect Analysis 
To uncover the dynamic process and underlying mechanisms through which the green data 
center policy affects corporate energy utilization efficiency, this study introduces executives’ green 
cognition and executives’ digital cognition as moderating variables and conducts corresponding 
tests. First, to determine the direction of the moderating effects of executives’ green cognition and 
executives’ digital cognition, an intuitive approach is to plot the moderation diagrams.

Figure 5. Moderating Effects Diagram 
 
In Figure 5, Panels (a), (b), and (c) illustrate the moderating effects of executives’ green 
cognition, executives’ digital cognition, and their joint moderation, respectively. As shown in Figure 
5(a), the slope of the regression line becomes markedly steeper as executives’ green cognition 
increases, providing preliminary evidence that executives’ green cognition positively strengthens 
the policy effect. Figure 5(b) indicates that when executives’ digital cognition is higher, the marginal 
impact of the green data center policy on corporate energy utilization efficiency becomes weaker, 
suggesting that digital cognition alone may attenuate the policy’s energy-saving and efficiency-
enhancing effect to some extent. Further, Figure 5(c) shows that when executives simultaneously 
exhibit high levels of green cognition and digital cognition, the policy’s positive effect on corporate 
energy utilization efficiency is strongest, indicating a clear synergistic moderating effect of the dual 
cognitive capabilities in the transmission of the policy effect. 
Building on this evidence, we conduct moderating-effect regressions, and the results are 
reported in Table 5. With respect to executives’ green cognition, the coefficient on the interaction 
term between the green data center policy and executives’ green cognition is significantly positive, 
indicating that executives’ green cognition plays a positive moderating role in the policy 
transmission process. This finding implies that, in firms where top managers strongly endorse green 
development concepts, the green data center policy is more likely to be interpreted as an institutional 
opportunity to improve energy allocation efficiency and build long-term competitive advantage. As 
a result, these firms tend to respond more proactively through strategic actions such as strengthening 
energy management, undertaking technological upgrading, and optimizing operational processes. 
By contrast, firms with lower levels of green cognition often struggle to translate policy signals into 
internal actions, and the extent to which policy dividends are realized is more limited. These results 
suggest that executives’ green cognition functions as an amplifier between policy implementation 
and improvements in corporate energy utilization efficiency. 

With respect to executives’ digital cognition, the coefficient on the interaction term between 
the green data center policy and executives’ digital cognition is significantly negative, indicating 
that executives’ digital cognition, when acting alone, exerts a dampening effect on the policy impact. 
This finding does not imply that digital cognition is inherently detrimental to firm development. 
Rather, it suggests that, in the absence of constraints from a green development orientation, a high 
level of digital cognition may induce firms to focus excessively on computing capacity expansion 
and business scale growth, while paying relatively less attention to energy constraints and energy-
efficiency optimization objectives. Particularly in the early stage of digital transformation, rapidly 
rising demand for computing power may be accompanied by a parallel increase in energy inputs, 
which can weaken policy effectiveness in the short run and provides indirect evidence of the 
potential risk of a rebound effect in the application of digital technologies. 
We further include the triple interaction term among the green data center policy, executives’ 
green cognition, and executives’ digital cognition to test their synergistic moderating effect. The 
results show that the coefficient on the triple interaction term is significantly positive at the 1 percent 
level, indicating that when executives possess strong green cognition and digital cognition 
simultaneously, the two cognitive structures are not substitutes but instead form a clear synergistic 
enabling mechanism. In this setting, executives’ green cognition provides a clear value orientation 
for improving energy utilization efficiency, whereas executives’ digital cognition provides effective 
technological tools and implementation pathways to achieve this goal. Their integration helps firms 
avoid a bias toward expansion over energy saving during digital transformation. By promoting deep 
integration between green and digital technologies, firms can more fully translate the institutional 
potential embedded in the green data center policy into tangible improvements in internal energy 
management, thereby significantly strengthening the policy’s positive effect on corporate energy 
utilization efficiency. Overall, the impact of the green data center policy on corporate energy 
utilization efficiency is neither linear nor homogeneous. Policy effectiveness depends to a large 
extent on the configuration of the executive team’s cognitive structure. Digital cognition or green 
cognition in a single dimension is insufficient to fully unlock policy dividends. Only when green 
development orientation and digital capabilities are effectively aligned and coordinated can the 
green data center policy deliver its maximum enabling effect.

4.4. Heterogeneity Analysis 
To further reveal the context dependence of the green data center policy’s effect on corporate 
energy utilization efficiency, we conduct subgroup analyses from three dimensions: macro-level 
regional resource endowments, meso-level market structure, and micro-level corporate life-cycle 
stage. Table 6 reports the estimation results of the heterogeneity analyses. 
4.4.1. Resource Endowment Type 
Columns (1) and (2) of Table 6 examine heterogeneity by city resource endowment. The results 
show that in resource-based cities, the green data center policy has a significantly positive effect on 
corporate energy utilization efficiency, whereas in non-resource-based cities the enabling effect is 
not statistically significant. One possible explanation is that resource-based cities have long relied 
on inputs of energy and mineral resources to drive economic growth and therefore tend to have 
industrial structures with higher shares of energy-intensive and high-emission sectors. Extensive 
energy use is more pronounced, implying greater scope for efficiency improvement prior to policy 
implementation. By promoting digital infrastructure development and the adoption of energy 
management technologies, the green data center policy provides firms with a practical pathway to 
improve production methods and enhance energy allocation efficiency, making the policy effect 
more likely to materialize. In addition, resource-based cities often have comparative advantages in 
energy supply and related supporting facilities, which eases factor constraints during policy 
implementation and facilitates deeper integration of digital technologies with energy systems, 
thereby strengthening support for corporate energy utilization efficiency improvement. By contrast, 
non-resource-based cities tend to have more diversified industrial structures and relatively higher 
baseline energy utilization efficiency, leaving less room for marginal improvement. Moreover, the 
policy effect may be diluted by other development factors, making it harder for the green data center 
policy to generate statistically significant impacts. 
4.4.2. Market Structure Characteristics 

Columns (3) and (4) of Table 6 reflect the role of market structure in shaping policy 
effectiveness. The results indicate that the policy significantly improves corporate energy utilization 
efficiency in competitive industries, whereas the effect is not significant in regulated industries, 
suggesting that market structure characteristics may constrain the extent to which policy incentives 
translate into efficiency gains. A plausible reason is that firms in competitive industries face stronger 
survival pressures and tighter cost constraints, and thus have stronger incentives to use digital 
technologies to optimize production processes and improve energy utilization efficiency in order to 
maintain competitive advantage. In contrast, regulated industries typically have higher entry barriers 
and more stable profit expectations. Firms’ operations are more strongly shaped by administrative 
regulation and institutional protection, and their responses to cost pressures and efficiency 
improvement are relatively sluggish, thereby weakening responsiveness to policy incentives. 
4.4.3. Corporate Life Cycle 
According to corporate life-cycle theory, firms at different developmental stages face 
fundamentally different resource constraints, governance structures, and strategic priorities, which 
creates heterogeneous environments for policy transmission and implementation. Following the 
approach of Liang et al. (2019), we classify sample firms into three stages, growth, maturity, and 
decline, using a composite scoring method based on four dimensions: sales revenue growth, retained 
earnings ratio, capital expenditure ratio, and firm age. Columns (5) to (7) of Table 6 report the 
subgroup regression results. The green data center policy exerts the strongest effect on corporate 
energy utilization efficiency among mature-stage firms, while the effect is not significant for 
growth-stage or decline-stage firms. This pattern may reflect that mature firms typically have robust 
cash flows and well-developed management systems, enabling them to absorb the high upfront costs 
associated with early-stage digital transformation and to achieve deeper coupling between green 
cognition and digital technologies. By contrast, growth-stage firms often prioritize market 
expansion and scale growth and may face resource misallocation with respect to long-term strategic 
investments such as energy-efficiency management. Decline-stage firms, meanwhile, are 
constrained by aging technologies and equipment as well as insufficient transformation momentum, 
making it difficult for them to improve energy utilization efficiency through policy guidance.

4.5.1. Mechanism Effects 
To further unpack the internal logic through which the green data center policy enhances 
corporate energy utilization efficiency, we examine two dimensions, namely corporate sustainability 
governance and green resource allocation. We select firms’ ESG performance and green investment 
as the key mechanism variables and, following Jiang Ting (2022), specify the following mechanism

In this framework, the mechanism variable Mit includes firms’ ESG performance (ESG) and 
green investment (Gis). ESG performance measures a firm’s overall performance in environmental 
responsibility, social responsibility, and corporate governance. Following Liu et al. (2026), we 
quantify ESG performance using the Huazheng ESG rating. Specifically, we map the Huazheng 
ESG grades from C to AAA to integer scores from 1 to 9 in ascending order, where a higher value 
indicates better ESG performance. Green investment captures firms’ resource allocation choices 
during the green transition. Drawing on Zhang et al. (2019), we proxy green investment by the share 
of expensed green investment in total green investment, which enables us to identify the incentive 
effect of the green data center policy on firms’ green investment behavior. All other variables are 
defined consistently with Model (1). 
Table 7 shows that the coefficients of the green data center policy on both mechanism variables are 
significantly positive at the 5 percent level. This indicates that the policy improves corporate energy 
utilization efficiency through two complementary channels: enabling firms to enhance ESG 
performance and inducing firms to increase green investment. On the one hand, as a key benchmark 
for greening digital infrastructure, the green data center policy continuously sends firms clear and 
stable signals regarding green governance through institutional arrangements. Under an institutional 
environment that combines regulatory constraints with reputational incentives, firms are more likely 
to embed green development objectives into corporate governance and strategic decision-making. 
This promotes systematic improvements in environmental responsibility, social responsibility, and 
the standardization of internal governance, thereby enhancing overall ESG performance. Because 
ESG performance exhibits institutional stickiness and path dependence, improvements in ESG 
typically reflect long-run adjustments in governance structure, managerial practices, and strategic 

orientation. As ESG performance improves, firms’ energy management systems are strengthened, 
environmental information transparency increases, and internal governance frictions are gradually 
reduced. These changes make the allocation of energy inputs more standardized and efficient, 
providing a stable governance foundation for sustained improvements in energy utilization 
efficiency (Wang et al., 2025). On the other hand, the green data center policy provides strong 
incentives for green investment by improving the availability of green technologies and lowering 
the cost of allocating green inputs. Under policy guidance and competitive pressure, firms tend to 
increase investment in energy-saving equipment, green process retrofits, and clean energy 
substitution to meet stricter requirements for energy efficiency and low-carbon performance. 
Compared with ESG performance, green investment is more adjustable and stage specific, allowing 
firms to upgrade technologies and reshape production processes within a shorter time horizon. 
Increased green investment facilitates deep optimization of production processes (Zhang et al., 2024) 
and accelerates the low-carbon transition of the energy consumption structure, curbing high-energy-
consumption and high-emission activities at the source (Zhang and Jin, 2023). As a result, firms can 
achieve simultaneous improvements in the efficiency of energy inputs and outputs in the short to 
medium term (Dong et al., 2024). 
It is important to note that although ESG performance and green investment are both responses 
to the green data center policy, they differ meaningfully in economic content and operating 
mechanisms. ESG performance reflects a governance logic, emphasizing a firm’s comprehensive 
governance quality in environmental responsibility, social responsibility, and corporate governance, 
and it more strongly captures a long-run value orientation associated with institutional building, 
strategic direction, and managerial standardization (Xie et al., 2024). In contrast, green investment 
follows an investment logic, focusing on capital allocation to specific projects and technologies 
during the green transition, and it primarily reflects short-term and medium-term resource allocation 
decisions. Taken together, across different time horizons, the green data center policy improves 
corporate energy utilization efficiency through two key channels, enabling firms to enhance ESG 
performance and inducing firms to increase green investment. Through these pathways, the policy 
translates external institutional incentives into internal drivers of energy-efficiency improvement, 
thereby strengthening energy utilization efficiency under the joint advancement of greening and 
digitalization.

4.5.2. Policy Diffusion Effects 
As an important institutional arrangement guiding the greening transition of digital 
infrastructure, the green data center pilot policy has adopted a gradual reform approach since 2018, 
expanding from selected points to broader coverage through batch-based enlargement. By 2024, six 
batches of pilot cities had been implemented. Although the preceding analysis confirms the overall 
effectiveness of the policy, it remains necessary to test whether, during the dynamic process of 
continuous expansion, the policy effect can be released consistently across regions and stages and 
thereby generate a diffusion effect with broader applicability. To this end, taking the approval batch 
as the time marker, we sequentially include the first-batch pilot cities through the first six batches 
of pilot cities in the treated group and use non-pilot cities as the control group. The corresponding 
results are summarized in Table 8. Table 8 shows that, across the stepwise regressions that expand 
the treated group from the first batch to the first six batches, the estimated coefficient on the core 
explanatory variable remains significantly positive at the 1 percent level. This evidence indicates 
that the green data center policy is not a short-term or localized institutional dividend. Rather, it 
delivers robust effectiveness across a broad spatial scope and over a long time horizon, 
demonstrating clear diffusion value and spillover potential. A further comparison of the coefficients 
across batches suggests that policy effectiveness follows a nonlinear pattern as additional pilot 
batches are incorporated, increasing initially and then declining thereafter. In the early stage of the 
program, the estimated coefficient rises as the pilot coverage expands, reflecting a pronounced 
institutional learning effect. As computing nodes and green standards are initially established, 
demonstration effects begin to emerge. Early pilot cities accumulate replicable experience in 
technological problem-solving, supply-chain coordination, and innovation in energy management 
models. During this phase, the greening upgrade of digital infrastructure accelerates, and the release 
of scale effects further amplifies the marginal impact of the policy on corporate energy utilization 
efficiency. 
In the subsequent phase of moderation, as the pilot program expands further from the third to 
the sixth batch, the estimated coefficient remains significantly positive but shows a modest decline 
in magnitude. Two mechanisms may account for this pattern. First, consistent with diminishing 
marginal returns, as policy coverage approaches saturation, firms’ sensitivity to external policy 
incentives may weaken temporarily. Second, later-admitted regions may differ from the first-batch 
benchmark cities in resource endowments, digital economy foundations, and the degree of market 
development, which can constrain the efficiency with which policy dividends are converted into 
improvements in corporate energy utilization efficiency.

5. Conclusions and Policy Implications 
As a key institutional arrangement that promotes deep integration between greening and 
digitalization, the green data center policy plays an important role in improving corporate energy 
utilization efficiency. Using Chinese A-share listed firms from 2012 to 2024 as the study sample 
and applying a staggered-adoption difference-in-differences design, this study systematically 
examines the mechanisms through which the green data center policy affects corporate energy 
utilization efficiency and yields the following main findings. (1) The green data center policy 
significantly improves corporate energy utilization efficiency. The underlying mechanisms operate 
primarily through two channels: enabling firms to enhance ESG performance and inducing firms to 
increase green investment. Moreover, policy effectiveness is context dependent with respect to 
regional resource endowments, market structure characteristics, and corporate life-cycle stage. 
Specifically, the policy effect is more pronounced in resource-based cities, in competitive industries, 
and among mature-stage firms. (2) Executive green cognition positively moderates the enabling 
effect of the green data center policy on corporate energy utilization efficiency, whereas executive 
digital cognition exhibits a negative moderating effect when considered in isolation. When the two 
cognitive capabilities operate jointly, executive green cognition effectively offsets the negative 

moderation associated with executive digital cognition and further strengthens the policy’s positive 
impact on corporate energy utilization efficiency. (3) As the pilot program expands across batches, 
the policy’s diffusion effect follows a nonlinear pattern, increasing initially and then declining 
thereafter. 
Based on these findings, this study offers the following policy implications.  
(1) Governments and relevant regulators should leverage high-quality green digital 
infrastructure development to convert policy dividends into firms’ sustained energy-efficiency 
competitiveness. They should accelerate the greening upgrade of digital infrastructure and promote 
deeper integration between greening and digitalization, while fully positioning green data centers 
as demonstration leaders. This approach strengthens green data centers’ hub role in advancing the 
dual-carbon agenda, supporting new industrialization, and enabling the Digital China strategy. 
Regulatory authorities should also expand the scale and coverage of pilot programs and support data 
center operators in delivering modular energy-efficiency solutions tailored to firms of different sizes, 
thereby improving service fit and accessibility and facilitating scalable, replicable practices as well 
as experience sharing. In addition, data center operators and participating firms should strengthen 
energy-efficiency collaboration so that green data centers evolve from infrastructure providers into 
energy-efficiency service enablers. Specifically, operators should integrate more deeply with firms’ 
energy-use systems and enable data interoperability and functional integration through energy 
management platforms and application programming interfaces, providing value-added services 
such as real-time energy monitoring, carbon footprint tracking, energy-efficiency diagnostics, and 
optimization recommendations. Standard-setting bodies and regulators should further accelerate the 
issuance of technical specifications and unified interface standards for green computing services to 
lower firms’ access barriers. Together, these actions strengthen the transmission pathway from 
greener computing power to more efficient energy use and translate policy dividends into durable 
firm-level advantages. 
(2) Firms, regulators, and industry associations should promote coordinated upgrading of 
executives’ cognition and capabilities to unlock the maximum enabling effect of the green data 
center policy. First, training providers and relevant authorities should strengthen executives’ 
strategic literacy in both green development and digital transformation by offering targeted 
programs on green strategy and digital leadership through channels such as the State-owned Assets 
Supervision and Administration Commission and industry associations. These programs can 
reinforce executives’ commitment to green development and help them internalize sustainability as 
a foundational logic for digital transformation. Meanwhile, industry associations and training 
institutions should design and scale contextualized, modular digital application workshops centered 
on operational scenarios such as energy saving, emission reduction, and carbon management, 
thereby helping executives identify implementable pathways through which digitalization improves 
energy utilization efficiency and reducing misalignment caused by cognitive disconnects or 
capability mismatches. Second, firms should build composite managerial and organizational 
mechanisms by prioritizing executives with both environmental responsibility awareness and digital 
competence and by establishing dedicated roles such as a Green Digital Officer or cross-functional 
green digital task forces to coordinate energy, digital, and ESG strategies, break down silos, and 
ensure strategic alignment. Third, firms should institutionalize long-term mechanisms that embed 
green principles across the full life cycle of digital system development and energy management, 
integrating them into system design, operational scheduling, energy-efficiency evaluation, and 

energy-use decision-making. This institutionalization supports a virtuous cycle in which green 
development guides digitalization and digitalization enables greening, thereby turning external 
policy incentives into endogenous drivers of energy-efficiency improvement. 
(3) Policymakers and local governments should implement differentiated, targeted approaches 
to move the green data center policy from localized demonstrations toward broad and efficient 
coverage. For groups that respond strongly to the policy, including resource-based cities, 
competitive industries, and mature-stage firms, governments and financial institutions should 
strengthen bundled incentives such as tax preferences, green credit, and targeted subsidies. These 
incentives can support deeper integration with green data centers and encourage these actors to 
participate in developing and refining standards for green computing services and energy-efficiency 
evaluation systems, thereby creating replicable benchmarks and amplifying demonstration effects. 
For groups with weaker policy responses, such as non-resource-based cities, regulated industries, 
and growth-stage or decline-stage firms, governments and support agencies should prioritize 
capability building through technical assistance, green transition diagnostics, and digital energy-
saving training to address gaps in cognition and implementation capacity. In parallel, policymakers 
should lower access barriers to green cloud services for growth-stage firms and allow longer retrofit 
transition windows for decline-stage firms to enhance policy inclusiveness. Finally, central 
authorities should grant greater autonomy to local governments so that they can develop region-
specific collaborative implementation plans aligned with local industrial structures, energy systems, 
and digital foundations. Local governments should also establish cross-city and cross-park 
platforms for green technology sharing and experience exchange to accelerate the diffusion of best 
practices and support a shift from point-based breakthroughs to area-wide coordination. 
 
Data availability 
Firm-level data are primarily obtained from the CSMAR database and firms’ annual reports. City-
level variables are compiled mainly from publicly available information released on the official 
website of the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and from various editions of the 
China City Statistical Yearbook.

A sustainable and secure load 
management model for green 
cloud data centres
Deepika Saxena 1,2*, Ashutosh Kumar Singh 1*, Chung‑Nan Lee 3 & Rajkumar Buyya 4
The massive upsurge in cloud resource demand and inefficient load management stave off the 
sustainability of Cloud Data Centres (CDCs) resulting in high energy consumption, resource 
contention, excessive carbon emission, and security threats. In this context, a novel Sustainable 
and Secure Load Management (SaS-LM) Model is proposed to enhance the security for users with 
sustainability for CDCs. The model estimates and reserves the required resources viz., compute, 
network, and storage and dynamically adjust the load subject to maximum security and sustainability. 
An evolutionary optimization algorithm named Dual-Phase Black Hole Optimization (DPBHO) is 
proposed for optimizing a multi-layered feed-forward neural network and allowing the model to 
estimate resource usage and detect probable congestion. Further, DPBHO is extended to a Multi-
objective DPBHO algorithm for a secure and sustainable VM allocation and management to minimize 
the number of active server machines, carbon emission, and resource wastage for greener CDCs. 
SaS-LM is implemented and evaluated using benchmark real-world Google Cluster VM traces. The 
proposed model is compared with state-of-the-arts which reveals its efficacy in terms of reduced 
carbon emission and energy consumption up to 46.9% and 43.9%, respectively with improved 
resource utilization up to 16.5%.
Nowadays, there is a strong tendency towards “digitization in everything and everything in digitization” across 
the globe which has increased cloud data centre (CDC) traffic exponentially. Likely, the high emission of green-
house gases such as carbon footprints along with heat generation and shared computing-derived multi-tenant 
environment puts a significant question on sustainability and security of CDCs. The electrical energy consump-
tion of CDCs would increase up to 15-fold by 2030, i.e., approximately 8 per cent of projected global demand 
which is estimated to account for more than 3.2 per cent of the total worldwide greenhouse gas ­emissions1. The 
power supply avenue has a huge impact on carbon footprint emission such as high carbon emitting source (for 
example, coal) dominates lower carbon sources such as renewable energy (for example, wind, sun) in carbon 
footprint ­production2,3. Therefore, by establishing the proactive sustainability and efficiency measures at incep-
tion, and leveraging the latest technology CDCs have to explore using renewable energy such as wind, hydro 
or solar to power data centres and optimising technology to improve its efficiency and operating temperature 
while reducing carbon ­emission4. Several factors contribute to the energy and carbon efficiency of ­CDCs5,6 which 
must be considered during physical resource distribution and management based on environmental criteria. 
These factors include higher average utilization of physical server machines via virtualization; green power sup-
ply to the servers employing renewable sources of energy for reduced carbon emission; improved power usage 
efficiency (PUE) of the servers to save potential carbon emission; energy-efficient utilization of server machines 
while delivering cloud services to the end-users7. Among these, the most significant factor is efficient manage-
ment of load while distributing physical resources which directly affects the server utilization, PUE and security 
of ­CDCs7,8. Nevertheless, while accomplishing a green cloud computing environment, an essential requirement 
of the cloud user i.e., security of application data during processing as well as storage should not be ­neglected9. 
Co-residency of multiple users sharing the same server machine maximizes the probability of security threats 
such as data hampering, leakage of sensitive information ­etc10. This gives a motivation to develop an effective 
solution for secure and sustainable cloud resource distribution and load management.

The major challenge entangled with developing such a solution is the trade-off about the contradictory 
objectives during load management. Undeniably, the cloud service provider aspires to maximize the revenues by 
distributing maximum workload on the minimum number of active servers to exhilarate energy efficiency and 
reduce power consumption costs while ignoring the security aspects during load execution. Such a distribution 
of resources allows multiple users to share the common physical machines and accelerates the probability of 
security breaches on VMs executing the workload of different users. Contrary to this, energy efficiency of the 
cloud environment descends and carbon footprint emission rises if the CSP minimizes sharing of the physical 
servers to strengthen the security of users’ workload.
In view of the aforementioned context, this article proposes a novel Secure and Sustainable Load Manage-
ment (SaS-LM) Model to minimize the security threats, power consumption, and carbon emission and maximize 
server resource utilization and PUE. This model analyses cloud workload in anticipation while addressing dif-
ferent resource utilization on virtual machines and manages the entire load while considering multiple factors 
related to security and sustainability. It employs a Multi-layered Feed Forward Neural Network (MFNN) as a 
workload analyser which is optimized by a newly developed Dual-Phase BlackHole Optimization (DPBHO) 
algorithm. Further, a secure and sustainable VM placement (VMP) is presented for optimized allocation of 
physical resource among VMs to serve the perspectives of both cloud user and service providers while procuring 
sustainability of CDCs. For the cloud users, it ingrains the secure placement of VMs by minimizing the prob-
ability of security breaches and reduces the operational cost of CDC for service provider by maximizing server 
resource utilization and minimizing power consumption. Also, the sustainability of the cloud environment is 
enhanced by improving power usage effectiveness and minimizing carbon footprint intensity.
The key contributions of the proposed work are fivefold:
•	 MFNN-based cloud workload resource usage analyser is developed to forecast resource usage in real-time 
with enhanced accuracy which triggers load shifting to alleviate the effect of over/under-load on the server 
before its actual occurrence and improve performance of CDC.
•	 A novel DPBHO algorithm is proposed for optimization of MFNN during cloud resource usage estimation. It 
is further extended to a multi-objective DPBHO (i.e., M-DPBHO) for placement of VMs subject to multiple 
constraints and objectives.
•	 Secure and sustainable VMP is proposed to procure sustainability, energy consumption and security of CDC, 
simultaneously serving the perspectives of both service provider as well as end-user.
•	 It facilitates the secure execution of user applications by minimizing the resource sharing among users of 
common physical server machines in real-time.
•	 The experimental simulation and evaluation of the proposed model by using a real benchmark dataset reveal 
that the proposed work outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of various performance metrics.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section “Results” discusses experimental set-up and results of 
workload prediction, resource utilization, power consumption, sustainability, security, and trade-off among 
the obtained results. The proposed method is discussed in Section “Method” includes Dual-phase Black-Hole 
Optimization, cloud workload usage analysis, secure and sustainable VM placement, and VM management and 
SaS-LM operational summary. The background and related discussion is given in Section “Background and 
discussion”. Finally, Section “Conclusion and future work” entails conclusive remarks and future scope of the 
proposed work.
Results
The simulation experiments are executed on a server machine assembled with two ­Intel® ­Xeon® Silver 4114 CPUs 
with 40 core processors and a 2.20 GHz clock speed. The server machine is deployed with 64-bit Ubuntu 16.04 
LTS, having main memory of 128 GB. The data centre environment included three different types of servers 
and four types of VMs configuration shown in Tables 1 and 2. The resource features like power consumption 
( PWmax, PWmin ), MIPS, RAM, and memory are taken from real server ­IBM11 configurations where S1 is ‘Pro-
LiantM110G5XEON3075’, S2 is ‘IBMX3250Xeonx3480’ and S3 is ‘IBM3550Xeonx5675’. The VMs configuration 
is inspired by the VM instances of the Amazon ­website12. Table 3 shows the experimental set-up parameters 
and their values.
Google Cluster Dataset (GCD) is utilized for performance estimation of SaS-LM and comparative approaches 
which contains resources CPU, memory, disk I/O request and resource usage information of 672,300 jobs exe-
cuted on 12,500 servers for the period of 29 ­days13. The CPU and memory utilization percentage of VMs are 
obtained from the given CPU and memory usage percentage for each task in every five minutes over period of 
twenty-four hours.
