Vol-04|Issue-12|December|Year-2024 International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)ISSN: 3049-2343
1. Introduction
1.1 Context and motivation
Data centers and telecom networks have shifted from being enabling back-office
systems to being “critical digital utilities” that shape national competitiveness, climate
outcomes, and citizen well-being. The growth of cloud services, AI training and
inference, and platform-mediated public services increases demand for reliable
compute, storage, and low-latency connectivity. This demand creates a direct
environmental footprint through electricity consumption and a significant indirect
footprint through embodied emissions in construction, cooling, and IT hardware. For
India, where a large share of demand growth occurs alongside rapidly expanding
digital public services, the environmental performance of digital infrastructure is
increasingly an economic and policy variable rather than an externality (DoT, 2018;
MeitY, 2020).
Digital inclusion remains the complementary constraint. Connectivity expansion does
not automatically translate into meaningful use: device affordability, accessibility,
quality of service, language and disability-inclusive design, and safety from cyber
harms are required for adoption. State-level variation is decisive because rights-of-
way, local power distribution conditions, public-service delivery readiness, and
skilling ecosystems differ substantially across states and UTs. In practice, the same
national program can yield widely different outcomes depending on state capacity and
local execution conditions, making a sub-national benchmark essential for actionable
policy design (DoT, 2024).
The motivation for an integrated benchmark is that “green data centers” and “digital
inclusion” are often treated as separate agendas with different metrics, institutional
owners, and financing pathways. ESG is sometimes limited to disclosure, while
inclusion is sometimes reduced to coverage counts. A cross-layer benchmark is
designed to connect upstream infrastructure and governance inputs to downstream
outcomes such as inclusion, productivity, resilience, and sustainability, thereby
improving decision relevance for both state governments and private infrastructure
investors.

Vol-04|Issue-12|December|Year-2024 International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)ISSN: 3049-2343
1.2 Research problem and objectives
The central research problem is the absence of a state/UT-level comparative
instrument that jointly evaluates green data center readiness and digital inclusion
maturity within a single ESG framework. Existing approaches tend to analyze data
center ecosystems as investment clusters, while treating inclusion as a telecom access
problem. This separation obscures cross-layer causality: for example, a state may
attract capacity yet underperform on sustainability due to weak KPI enforcement, or
may expand access yet lose trust due to cyber fraud and privacy harms. Such
dynamics motivate a unified benchmark that can diagnose gaps across policy,
infrastructure, standards, skills, adoption, and trust governance.
The study pursues four objectives. First, it operationalizes a strict Comparative &
Cross-Layer
framework
spanning
policy
and
regulation;
infrastructure;
data/standards/interoperability; talent and skilling; prosperity and sustainability;
innovation and investment; adoption/use-case maturity; and risk and trust governance.
Second, it benchmarks Indian state/UT pathways against G20 and BRICS archetypes,
focusing on transferable instruments and contextual constraints rather than “one-size-
fits-all” models. Third, it proposes a named readiness/transition index (G-DIISTI)
with explicit weights, scoring rubric, and evidence protocol suitable for open-source
updating. Fourth, it translates findings into recommendations and a phased roadmap
that supports both hub states and inclusion-priority states.
The policy significance is practical: a state-level benchmark can guide incentive
design, public procurement, permitting conditions, and skilling investments. It can
also help investors compare ESG and trust maturity across locations and reduce the
risk of stranded assets driven by tightening sustainability and cyber compliance
requirements in global supply chains.
1.3 Research questions and propositions
RQ1 asks which cross-layer factors best explain variation in green data center
readiness and digital inclusion maturity across Indian states and UTs. The benchmark
expects that infrastructure readiness (power reliability, fiber density, land facilitation)
is necessary but not sufficient, and that standards and governance maturity mediate
the translation of infrastructure into sustainability and inclusion outcomes.

Vol-04|Issue-12|December|Year-2024 International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)ISSN: 3049-2343
RQ2 asks which policy instruments and standards from G20 and BRICS archetypes
are transferable to Indian state contexts, and under what constraints. The benchmark
expects that measurement and reporting standards (e.g., definitional alignment for
PUE/WUE
and
incident
reporting
playbooks)
are
highly
transferable,
while
enforcement intensity and centralized allocation mechanisms require adaptation to
Indian institutional and market structures.
RQ3 asks how a readiness/transition index can be designed using open sources
without relying on proprietary datasets. The benchmark proposes that ordinal,
evidence-based scoring can complement quantitative indicators for comparability and
transparency, provided a consistent rubric and validation protocol are applied.
From these questions, two working propositions are specified. Proposition P1: states
that embed measurable ESG KPIs and cyber baselines into incentives and permitting
will achieve faster improvements in sustainability outcomes than states relying on
voluntary disclosure. Proposition P2: states that integrate cyber-safe service delivery
(privacy-by-design, fraud reduction, grievance redressal) into inclusion programs will
show higher adoption depth and resilience than states focusing mainly on connectivity
expansion.
1.4 Scope, definitions, and delimitations
The scope includes green data centers as the core compute and storage infrastructure
underpinning telecom and digital services, and digital inclusion as the meaningful
capability of households, citizens, and firms to access and use digital services safely.
Green data center performance is defined through a lifecycle-aware ESG lens that
includes operational efficiency (energy and water), renewable procurement pathways,
and governance measures that ensure transparency and auditability.
The benchmark is state/UT-focused but includes a national ecosystem layer because
electricity market rules, national missions, and statutory governance frameworks
shape the feasible policy space. International benchmarks are used as archetypes
rather than as strict comparators, with the emphasis placed on instruments and design
patterns that are credible for Indian states. The results section includes an illustrative
scorecard rather than an authoritative ranking for all states, reflecting the design intent
to provide a replicable template.

Vol-04|Issue-12|December|Year-2024 International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)ISSN: 3049-2343
The benchmark does not claim to estimate precise emissions or economic impacts at
the state level, unless they are directly traceable to publicly available datasets. Where
precision is not defensible from open sources, the analysis employs structured ordinal
scoring
with
explicit
evidence
notes,
thereby
prioritizing
transparency
and
updateability over over-confident quantification.
1.5 Structure of the report
Section 2 establishes the conceptual foundation linking ESG, green data center
performance, inclusion theory, and cyber-trust governance. Section 3 outlines the G20
and BRICS landscape through five archetypes and identifies transferable instruments.
Section 4 provides an India national overview of telecom, data center, energy, and
governance conditions. Section 5 develops a state maturity clustering to interpret
regional divergence. Section 6 deepens the cyber governance theme within ESG,
highlighting secure efficiency, interoperability, and resilience.
Section 7 specifies the methods, including open-source data collection, variable
construction, a scoring rubric, and the G-DIISTI index with weights and formulae.
Section 8 presents results through tables and figures embedded alongside Analysis.
Section 9 discusses implications and provides short cases of policy transferability and
contextual limits across India, G20, and BRICS. Sections 10 and 11 provide
recommendations and a phased roadmap. Section 12 concludes, and the reference list
provides traceable sources in Harvard style (without hyperlinks).
2. Conceptual and Theoretical Foundation
2.1 ESG framing for telecom and digital infrastructure
ESG in telecom and digital infrastructure is a strategic governance lens rather than a
narrow disclosure function. Environmental performance is dominated by electricity
consumption and cooling for data centers and telecom network equipment, while also
including embodied impacts in construction, power distribution, and IT hardware.
Social performance encompasses coverage, affordability, accessibility for vulnerable
groups, and the capability to use services productively. Governance performance
includes compliance integrity, risk management, transparency, cyber resilience, and
privacy stewardship that protects users and sustains trust (SEBI, 2021).

Vol-04|Issue-12|December|Year-2024 International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)ISSN: 3049-2343
An India-first ESG framing places development outcomes at the center. Digital
infrastructure is increasingly tied to public service delivery (health, education,
welfare), small-firm productivity, and resilience to shocks. Consequently, ESG
evaluation must ask whether infrastructure growth improves inclusion, reduces
service inequities, and supports adaptation to climate risks. This turns ESG into a
cross-layer system property that can be influenced by state-level permitting,
procurement, and mission implementation.
A practical implication is that ESG for digital infrastructure requires “measurability.”
Voluntary claims are insufficient when data centers scale rapidly: operators, states,
and financiers require comparable KPIs and evidence of governance controls. This
motivates the index design that explicitly links upstream KPIs and controls to
downstream inclusion and resilience outcomes.
Carbon, Energy, and Efficiency Engineering for ESG-Grade Green Data Centres:
A core subtheme consolidates energy efficiency and carbon accounting into a
measurable ESG “E” pillar for data centres, linking technical efficiency (e.g.,
workload placement and thermal scheduling) to auditable benchmarks. Indian
guidance on efficient data-centre practices provides a baseline for operational controls
and measurement choices (BEE, 2010), while updated grid-emissions baselines
enable
state-level
and
national
carbon
intensity
attribution
(CEA,
2024).
Complementary international best-practice guidance strengthens comparability across
G20/BRICS
contexts
by
standardising
efficiency
actions
and
procurement
expectations for servers and data centres (JRC, 2024; UNEP and U4E, 2024). In this
cluster, optimisation research strengthens the “innovation” pathway: quantum-
inspired formulations for energy-aware VM placement and thermal-aware scheduling
operationalise energy reduction as a formal objective function rather than an
aspirational target (Pasupuleti, 2024i; Pasupuleti, 2024j).
A further theoretical contribution is the treatment of energy-efficient operations as a
decision science problem under uncertainty and constraints. OR and stochastic
programming perspectives frame energy, carbon, cost, and SLA trade-offs as solvable
resource-allocation regimes (Pasupuleti, 2021d; Pasupuleti, 2021f; Pasupuleti, 2021g).

Vol-04|Issue-12|December|Year-2024 International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)ISSN: 3049-2343
Deep RL is positioned as an approximate dynamic programming approach for real-
time control, which matters for “always-on” infrastructures where load, tariffs, and
cooling conditions vary rapidly (Pasupuleti, 2021b; Pasupuleti, 2022c). Policy
implications follow directly: ESG benchmarking can move beyond narrative
disclosures by embedding verifiable performance indicators tied to grid factors,
procurement rules, and optimisation-derived savings, enabling consistent cross-
jurisdiction reporting (CEA, 2024; UNEP and U4E, 2024).
Telemetry-to-Decision Pipelines: Forecasting, Econometrics, and Closed-Loop Green
Operations:
A second subtheme clusters data pipelines, forecasting, and control as the operational
backbone
that
turns
green
ambitions
into
continuously-managed
outcomes.
Digitalisation increases energy demand in complex ways, making measurement
granularity and feedback design central to sustainability governance (OECD, 2017).
Big-data telemetry pipelines for cloud/network signals provide the evidence layer for
KPI computation, anomaly detection, and optimisation triggers (Pasupuleti, 2024a;
Pasupuleti, 2022a). Forecasting is treated as a strategic enabler because greener
operations depend
on anticipating
demand
peaks
to avoid
inefficient
over-
provisioning;
hybrid
comparisons
of classical
time-series
and
deep learning
approaches formalise model selection and reproducibility as part of the sustainability
toolchain (Pasupuleti, 2024d).
Methodologically, this subtheme extends to econometric demand modelling and
simulation-based control. Comparative econometric workflows offer interpretable,
audit-friendly estimates that can be mapped to ESG indicators (e.g., energy per unit
demand served) and to “S” outcomes such as service availability supporting inclusion
(Pasupuleti, 2024f). Co-simulation of cloud and network control loops elevates
governance from offline reporting to real-time system design, helping policy makers
and operators test interventions before deployment (Pasupuleti, 2024c). Research
implications include treating telemetry lineage, model risk, and update cadence as
ESG-relevant
(because
they
determine
whether
reported
metrics
are
stable,

Vol-04|Issue-12|December|Year-2024 International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)ISSN: 3049-2343
comparable, and decision-useful), while the policy implication is that state-level ESG
benchmarks should require minimum telemetry and model-governance standards to
prevent “greenwashing by measurement gaps” (OECD, 2017; Pasupuleti, 2024a).
Climate-Resilient Siting and Spatial Risk Governance for Data Centres:
A third subtheme frames where data centres are built as a coupled sustainability–
resilience decision, especially under intensifying climate and flood hazards. State-
level data-centre policies create the immediate institutional context for siting,
approvals, and infrastructure commitments (Government of Tamil Nadu, 2021;
Government of Uttar Pradesh, 2021). Research in this cluster formalises siting as a
multi-criteria decision problem that integrates cost, risk, and sustainability, using GIS-
based screening and hydrologic simulation to avoid maladaptive lock-in (Pasupuleti,
2022e; Pasupuleti, 2022b). A climate- and flood-aware siting framework extends this
logic by explicitly incorporating flood exposure and long-horizon climate-driven
precipitation extremes into early-stage infrastructure choices (Pasupuleti, 2024b).
This subtheme also connects to benchmark design: resilience can be represented as an
ESG-linked capability because climate disruptions affect continuity of essential
digital
services.
Spatial
analytics
for
energy-efficient
infrastructure
supports
transparent regional comparisons and scenario communication to stakeholders
(Pasupuleti, 2024g). National indicator systems (e.g., SDG-linked state indices) can
be used to align green data-centre expansion with broader development priorities and
regional equity objectives (NITI Aayog, 2024). Policy implications are multi-sectoral:
siting rules can require climate-risk stress testing and disclosure, while procurement
guidance can encode resilience expectations into contracts, improving comparability
between Indian states and peer economies across G20/BRICS (UNEP and U4E, 2024;
Government of Telangana, n.d.).
Cybersecurity,
Data
Protection,
and
Compliance-by-Design
as
ESG
“G”
Infrastructure:

Vol-04|Issue-12|December|Year-2024 International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)ISSN: 3049-2343
A fourth subtheme treats cybersecurity and privacy governance as a foundational
condition for digital inclusion and for credible ESG disclosure, because insecure
infrastructure undermines trust, service continuity, and legal compliance. National and
transnational regimes establish the compliance perimeter: incident reporting and
operational controls (CERT-In, 2022), updated cybersecurity governance frameworks
(NIST, 2024), and strengthened EU-wide cyber resilience requirements (EU, 2022).
In parallel, privacy and data protection laws shape cross-border data handling and
accountability (Government of Brazil, 2018; Government of South Africa, 2013;
MeitY, 2023). This regulatory stack is directly relevant to a G20/BRICS benchmark
because it affects the feasibility of comparable reporting and the portability of
governance controls.
Research
contributions
in
this
cluster
translate
governance
into
deployable
mechanisms.
Policy-as-code
is
positioned
as
an
instrument
for
enforceable
compliance and managerial control in cloud operations, converting rules into
automated checks and remediation (Pasupuleti, 2022d). Earlier work integrates RL-
based operations with policy constraints, framing “safe optimisation” as a governance
requirement rather than a technical preference (Pasupuleti, 2021c; Pasupuleti, 2021e).
More recent designs integrate telemetry and policy engines to support safe, auditable
resource
management
loops—important
for
ESG assurance
because
it
links
operational evidence to control actions (Pasupuleti, 2024h). Policy implications
include recommending minimum cyber/privacy control baselines as part of state ESG
scoring, ensuring that greener and more inclusive digital infrastructure is also trusted
and legally durable (CERT-In, 2022; NIST, 2024).
Digital Inclusion Metrics and State-Level ESG Benchmarking Across G20 and
BRICS:
A fifth subtheme integrates digital inclusion (“S”) with ESG measurement,
operationalising how green infrastructure expansion supports equitable connectivity
outcomes. National communications policy and broadband mission planning create

Vol-04|Issue-12|December|Year-2024 International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)ISSN: 3049-2343
the domestic policy logic for inclusion-oriented infrastructure rollouts (DoT, 2018;
DoT, 2024). Measurement systems then provide benchmark-ready indicators: the ICT
Development Index supports cross-country comparability, while national dashboards
and regulator statistics support within-country, state-level monitoring of access and
service performance (ITU, 2024; USOF, 2024; TRAI, 2024a; TRAI, 2024b). ESG
reporting requirements for listed entities provide governance templates for disclosure
structure and materiality—useful when adapting ESG logic to digital infrastructure
operators and state benchmarking frameworks (SEBI, 2021).
Methodologically, this subtheme benefits from transparency and ESG analytics
traditions that separate reported performance from explained performance. Work on
transparency and ESG-linked valuation dynamics motivates a benchmarking stance
where disclosures, governance quality, and performance metrics are analysed jointly,
rather than treating ESG as a single composite score (Pasupuleti, 2023j; Pasupuleti,
2023k). Demand modelling and forecasting can connect inclusion targets to capacity
planning, estimating how increased access changes network and data-centre loads,
and how to scale sustainably without carbon rebound (Pasupuleti, 2024f; OECD,

benchmark can use harmonised indicator families (access, affordability proxies,

2.2 Green data center performance metrics and lifecycle lens
Green data center evaluation is commonly structured around operational metrics such
as Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE), and
renewable energy factor or equivalent measures of low-carbon electricity procurement.
International best practice guidance emphasizes that PUE alone is insufficient because
it can be improved while absolute consumption rises, and because cooling
optimization may shift burdens to water consumption or local thermal impacts. A
balanced KPI set is therefore necessary for credible ESG benchmarking (European
Commission JRC, 2024; UNEP-U4E, 2024).

A lifecycle lens distinguishes operational emissions from embodied emissions in
concrete, steel, electrical infrastructure, and IT equipment. For India, operational
emissions depend heavily on grid emissions intensity and access to firm renewable
procurement. The Central Electricity Authority baseline emissions database provides
traceable factors and methodological guidance used in accounting and project
baselines, enabling consistent estimation approaches where states choose to report or
model impacts (CEA, 2024).
The lifecycle perspective also elevates circularity. Short refresh cycles for servers and
storage equipment can create material and e-waste burdens; governance therefore
needs to incorporate responsible procurement, asset tracking, refurbishment pathways,
and end-of-life management. These issues connect ESG directly to standards and
governance maturity, reinforcing the cross-layer logic of the benchmark.
2.3 Digital inclusion theory and capability constraints
Digital inclusion is treated as meaningful participation rather than mere connectivity.
Inclusion theory emphasizes capability: the ability of individuals and firms to convert
access into productive use. Capability is shaped by device affordability, language
accessibility, digital literacy, disability-inclusive design, and local relevance of
content and services. Connectivity expansion is a necessary condition, but it is not
sufficient for inclusion outcomes.
In telecom and digital infrastructure, inclusion is also shaped by reliability and latency.
Cloud-dependent services, telemedicine, digital learning, and MSME e-commerce
depend on service quality and continuity, not only coverage. State-level governance
influences these constraints through right-of-way execution, fiberization of towers,
public Wi-Fi and community networks, and local digital skilling ecosystems (DoT,
2024).
A further capability constraint arises from trust and safety. High-fraud environments
and fear of identity misuse can depress adoption, particularly among first-time users.
This places cyber governance and consumer protection mechanisms inside the
inclusion
framework,
strengthening
the
argument
for
integrating
cyber-trust
governance into ESG benchmarking rather than treating it as a separate domain.

2.4 Cyber-trust governance as an ESG enabler
Cyber-trust governance operates as an enabling constraint that affects both demand
and supply. On the supply side, weak cyber resilience increases downtime, incident
response costs, and reputational risks, which can reduce investment quality and raise
the cost of capital. On the demand side, cyber fraud, data breaches, and privacy harms
reduce confidence in digital services and can amplify exclusion among vulnerable
groups.
Governance instruments include baseline cyber frameworks, mandatory incident
reporting requirements, security auditing, and privacy law obligations. India’s
cybersecurity directions for service providers, intermediaries, and data centers create a
shared compliance layer for incident reporting and operational expectations (CERT-In,
2022). India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 provides a statutory
framework for lawful processing of personal data and accountability of data
fiduciaries (MeitY, 2023).
International reference instruments include NIST CSF 2.0 for cyber risk management
language and maturity (NIST, 2024) and the EU NIS2 directive regime for risk
management and incident reporting expectations (EU, 2022). The policy transfer
question is therefore not whether to adopt cyber governance, but how to implement it
proportionately across state capacities while ensuring measurable improvements in
trust and resilience.

Cross-layer analysis treats outcomes as end-states influenced by upstream inputs and

Comparative benchmarking against G20 and BRICS archetypes is used to avoid

vary and shape transferability.
2.6 Theoretical integration: infrastructure as platform, ESG as constraint, trust
as multiplier
The report integrates three theoretical ideas. First, digital infrastructure is treated as a
platform with network effects: investments in backbone connectivity and compute
capacity increase the value of digital services and attract complementary innovation.
Second, ESG is treated as a constraint set that determines the sustainability and
legitimacy of platform growth, particularly when energy and water demands rise.
Third, trust is treated as a multiplier that determines whether services are adopted and
whether inclusion is durable.
In this integrated view, cyber governance and privacy protections are not merely
defensive; they increase the “effective coverage” of digital infrastructure by raising
willingness to use services. Similarly, efficiency metrics and renewable procurement
increase the “effective sustainability” of infrastructure growth by reducing emissions
per unit of compute and service delivered. The cross-layer framework operationalizes
these theoretical relationships through measurable dimensions and evidence-based
scoring.
A policy implication is that the highest-leverage interventions are those that
simultaneously affect more than one layer: for example, standardizing KPI reporting
improves ESG comparability (governance) and also enables operational optimization
(infrastructure). Establishing shared security operations capacity improves reliability
(infrastructure), reduces cyber harms (governance), and increases adoption (inclusion).

3. G20 and BRICS Landscape
3.1 Archetype taxonomy for benchmarking
Benchmarking is organized around five archetypes that capture recurring patterns in
how economies regulate, finance, and operate digital infrastructure. The archetypes
are: (1) high-regulation high-trust; (2) fast-scaling innovation; (3) frugal/emerging-
economy scale; (4) security-first; and (5) ESG-integrated infrastructure. Each
archetype is characterized by typical policy tools (e.g., mandatory reporting,
performance standards, procurement rules), typical market structure (hyperscale
concentration versus diversified providers), and typical trust conditions (regulatory
legitimacy, privacy enforcement, cyber capacity).
Archetypes are used as reference models rather than as templates. The benchmark
extracts transferable instruments such as KPI definitions, reporting obligations,
procurement conditions, and skilling programs. It also identifies contextual limits
such as institutional capacity, electricity market structure, and legal constraints that
shape which elements are implementable at Indian state level.
A key insight from archetype comparison is that “green” and “secure” trajectories are
increasingly converging: measurement and reporting requirements for sustainability
often travel alongside cybersecurity requirements for critical infrastructure. This
convergence supports the report’s integration of cyber governance within ESG for
digital infrastructure.

3.3 Fast-scaling innovation archetype (illustrative: United States)
The fast-scaling innovation archetype couples high private investment in hyperscale
and cloud infrastructure with baseline standardization through frameworks and
procurement. The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 illustrates a governance
language used widely for structuring cyber risk management, enabling maturity-based
implementation without mandating a single technology stack (NIST, 2024). This
approach supports comparability in governance maturity while leaving room for
innovation.
For sustainability, innovation economies often rely on market mechanisms and
procurement constraints that encourage renewable energy procurement and efficiency
improvements. The relevant transfer lesson is that innovation speed and sustainability
integrity can be aligned when procurement and financing reward measurable
performance rather than headline commitments.
In Indian state contexts, NIST-like governance language is transferable through
procurement for public services and state data center operations. Contextual limits
include uneven cyber capacity across states and vendors, implying that shared
services and training infrastructure are needed to avoid creating compliance barriers
that reduce market competition and inclusion.
3.4 Frugal/emerging-economy scale archetype (illustrative: Brazil and South
Africa)
Frugal/emerging-economy scale builders face the dual constraint of rapid connectivity
expansion and limited fiscal space for large subsidies. Policy emphasis often shifts
toward regulatory clarity, competitive market structures, and targeted inclusion

programs. The sustainability challenge is that rapid expansion can lock in inefficient
practices unless standards and procurement constraints are adopted early.
For governance and trust, Brazil’s LGPD and South Africa’s POPIA illustrate data
protection regimes that articulate lawful processing conditions and user rights, with
institutional structures for oversight and enforcement that evolve over time
(Government of Brazil, 2018; Government of South Africa, 2013). These regimes
reinforce that inclusion gains can be undermined by privacy harms and mistrust, and
that governance clarity is therefore a development enabler.
For Indian states, the transfer lesson is that low-friction compliance tooling,
standardized templates, and public-facing grievance mechanisms can raise trust
without large fiscal burden. Contextual limits include variation in institutional
enforcement and the fragmentation of digital service delivery systems across
departments and vendors, which makes interoperability and governance coordination
particularly important.
3.5 Security-first archetype (illustrative: China; partially Russia)
The security-first archetype places sovereign control, localization, and operational
security at the center of digital infrastructure strategy. This often includes direct
governance over data flows and infrastructure siting decisions. In China’s case,
sustainability and performance constraints for large data centers have also been
emphasized through targets and standards related to efficiency for new facilities,
illustrating performance-based governance at scale.
The core transfer lesson is the integration of security, standardization, and
performance requirements into permitting and hub development. For Indian states, a
selective approach is appropriate: performance-based permitting and standardized
interconnectivity can be adopted without replicating centralized control over the
market.
Contextual limits are significant. India’s constitutional and institutional architecture
emphasizes contestable regulation and multi-stakeholder governance rather than
centralized allocation. Consequently, security-first features that rely on strict central
control are not fully transferable, but transparent performance standards and
coordinated infrastructure planning remain valuable design patterns.

4. India National Overview
4.1 National digital communications strategy and regulation
India’s national digital communications strategy positions broadband as a driver of
empowerment and economic modernization. The National Digital Communications
Policy 2018 articulates strategic objectives including universal broadband, investment
attraction, and improved service quality, and frames digital communications as
foundational infrastructure for economic and social goals (DoT, 2018). National
strategy also emphasizes right-of-way reform and institutional coordination as critical
implementation levers.
The National Broadband Mission 2.0 (Vision Document 2024–30) reinforces
inclusive growth and digital empowerment goals and stresses collaboration between
central government, states, local bodies, industry, and civil society (DoT, 2024). The

Vol-04|Issue-12|December|Year-2024 International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)ISSN: 3049-2343
mission’s focus on universal broadband and improved service delivery implies that
state-level execution capacity is central to outcomes, because right-of-way approvals,
fiber deployment, and local facilitation are largely executed at sub-national levels.
Regulatory institutions such as TRAI provide performance indicators and oversight
that support measurement and accountability. For benchmarking purposes, national
policy documents define goals and constraints, while regulator reports provide
comparable indicators of telecom sector performance that can inform inclusion and
infrastructure readiness dimensions (TRAI, 2024a).
4.2 Digital inclusion backbone: BharatNet and last-mile programs
BharatNet provides a state-linked infrastructure backbone by connecting Gram
Panchayats through optical fiber and enabling last-mile distribution through FTTH
and Wi‑Fi hotspots. Official dashboards and program pages track indicators such as
connected Gram Panchayats, fiber laid, and commissioned FTTH connections (USOF,
2024). These indicators provide measurable proxies for backbone readiness and the
ability to expand local service delivery, particularly in rural areas.
Inclusion performance depends on how backbone capacity is translated into usable
service availability in schools, health facilities, and community institutions. States
differ in their capability to integrate backbone connectivity with local service delivery
programs, including the creation of public Wi‑Fi hotspots, community access points,
and digital literacy interventions. Consequently, a benchmark must include both
supply-side indicators (backhaul and reliability) and demand-side signals (use-case
uptake and service outcomes).
Last-mile success also depends on institutional coordination across departments and
local bodies. Where right-of-way and local permits are delayed, the cost of inclusion
rises and service quality suffers. The benchmark therefore treats last-mile governance
capacity as part of the policy and adoption layers rather than as a purely technical
deployment variable.
4.3 Data center ecosystem and policy direction
India’s data center ecosystem has been shaped by the Draft Data Centre Policy 2020,
which proposes minimum standards for data center and data center park development
and emphasizes capacity building and the creation of an enabling environment for
investment (MeitY, 2020). State data center policies have emerged as complementary

Vol-04|Issue-12|December|Year-2024 International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)ISSN: 3049-2343
instruments, offering facilitation, infrastructure status, and targeted incentives to
attract investment and to develop local ecosystems.
The national policy layer is relevant because it sets expectations for standardized
infrastructure, security, and capacity building. At the same time, state-level policies
determine practical conditions: land availability, electricity supply facilitation, water
permissions, and local approval workflows. This creates a strong rationale for state-
level benchmarking, since policy variation can create materially different ESG and
cyber risk profiles for operators and for public-service delivery systems that depend
on data centers.
From an ESG perspective, the data center ecosystem has become a focal point for
measurable sustainability performance. The benchmark therefore emphasizes the
adoption of efficiency and water metrics, renewable procurement pathways, and
governance controls such as incident reporting readiness and privacy-compliant
operations for workloads that process personal data.
4.4 Energy, emissions, and green operations context
The environmental performance of data centers in India is shaped by both facility
efficiency and grid emissions intensity. The Central Electricity Authority publishes a
baseline carbon dioxide emissions database for the Indian power sector, providing
factors and methodological guidance that are widely used in emissions accounting and
project baselines (CEA, 2024). This enables consistent approaches to estimating
operational emissions when states and operators report electricity consumption or
when scenarios are modeled.
Energy efficiency guidance for Indian data centers has been documented through
initiatives linked to the Bureau of Energy Efficiency, including practices related to
cooling optimization, power distribution efficiency, monitoring, and management
(BEE, 2010). These documents provide credible and context-specific practices that
can be linked to procurement and incentive conditions in state policies. They also
support the operationalization of ESG requirements beyond headline commitments.
A major constraint for state-level planning is the coupling between data center loads
and grid reliability. In regions where distribution infrastructure is weak, backup
generation use can be higher, increasing emissions and local air quality impacts.
Therefore, state policies that promote data centers must align electricity facilitation

Vol-04|Issue-12|December|Year-2024 International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)ISSN: 3049-2343
with measurable efficiency targets and low-carbon procurement pathways to avoid
lock-in of high-emissions operational profiles.
4.5 Cybersecurity, privacy, and trust governance
India’s cyber governance stack includes mandatory incident reporting directions
applicable to service providers, intermediaries, data centers, and body corporates.
These directions specify operational obligations including incident reporting timelines
and logging expectations, and they strengthen the governance baseline for critical
digital infrastructure (CERT-In, 2022). For state benchmarking, incident reporting
readiness is a measurable governance variable that influences reliability, resilience,
and trust in digital services.
India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 provides a statutory framework for
processing digital personal data, defining accountability and user rights in digital
contexts (MeitY, 2023). While the Act is national, state programs that deliver services
or operate state data centers must align processes, contracts, and vendor governance
with the statutory requirements, particularly for consent, purpose limitation, and data
security safeguards.
From a comparative perspective, India’s governance stack can be benchmarked
against international frameworks such as NIST CSF 2.0 and the EU NIS2 regime
(NIST, 2024; EU, 2022). The benchmark treats these as reference points for maturity
rather than as direct compliance requirements, focusing on the adoption of governance
practices that are feasible for diverse state capacities.

Conversely, weak KPI transparency and governance can raise the cost of capital and
reduce investment quality. This makes ESG benchmarking a practical tool for
improving investment attractiveness while aligning infrastructure growth with
national sustainability goals.
A key implication is that state policy design should consider how incentives interact
with financing. Rather than offering generic subsidies, states can offer facilitation
conditional on verified KPIs, enabling financiers to price ESG performance and
supporting the emergence of an “ESG premium” for high-performing facilities.
4.7 Sub-national governance and implementation capacity
State/UT governance capacity shapes implementation outcomes even under national
missions. Right-of-way execution, land and utility coordination, local permitting, and
public procurement workflows are primarily sub-national. States also vary in their
ability to maintain shared platforms, coordinate incident response, and deploy digital
literacy programs. These differences can amplify or dampen the effectiveness of
national programs and market investment.
Implementation capacity is particularly important for ESG because ESG performance
is governance-intensive: it requires measurement, monitoring, and enforcement. A
state may attract data center investment, but without KPI reporting and water-risk
governance, environmental externalities can rise. Similarly, inclusion programs can
expand connectivity, but without cyber-safe service design and grievance mechanisms,
trust can decline and adoption can stagnate.
Therefore, the benchmark treats governance and capacity not as background variables
but as core dimensions. This enables tailored recommendations: hub states can move
quickly to performance-based ESG requirements, while inclusion-priority states can
focus on foundational capacity building and shared services that reduce the cost of
compliance and improve resilience.

State maturity clustering is performed as an interpretive layer that groups states by
ecosystem signals rather than by a single indicator. Signals include the presence and

reliability and cyber-safe inclusion programs; and special-context regions can
prioritize resilience-first, low-impact designs and hybrid connectivity strategies.
5.2 Leaders: multi-layer readiness with measurable ESG trajectory
Leader states typically combine clear facilitation regimes for data centers and cloud
services, strong metro and intercity fiber connectivity, and innovation ecosystems that
supply specialized talent. These states are more likely to host large facilities and to
attract global operators. As a result, leaders face early pressure to demonstrate ESG
performance through measurable efficiency KPIs, renewable procurement pathways,
and transparent reporting aligned with global investor expectations.
Leader states also tend to have stronger institutional capacity for governance:
dedicated IT departments, digital public service platforms, and coordination with
industry and academia. This capacity enables adoption of baseline cyber governance
through incident response readiness, security audits, and procurement standards. It
also supports interoperability for public services, which multiplies inclusion outcomes
and reduces fragmentation across departments and vendors.
From a benchmarking perspective, leader states are the highest-leverage sites for
national sustainability gains because marginal efficiency improvements at scale yield
large absolute reductions in emissions and water impacts. Therefore, policy
recommendations
for
leader
states
emphasize
performance-linked
incentives,

mandatory KPI reporting for incentivized facilities, and integration of cyber baselines
into permitting and procurement.
5.3 Emerging: rapid scale-up with partial ESG and trust gaps
Emerging states show strong intent and accelerating investment, often supported by
explicit policies and targeted industrial corridors. The ecosystem may include planned
data center parks, improved connectivity, and proactive facilitation. However,
operational ESG maturity can lag: renewable procurement pathways may be
underdeveloped, water risk governance may not be integrated into permitting, and
KPI monitoring capacity may be limited.
Digital inclusion in emerging states often improves through national backbone
programs, but service quality and local digital capability gaps can limit meaningful
adoption. These states frequently experience a “mid-layer gap” where infrastructure
supply improves faster than interoperability, skilling, and institutional governance.
This can lead to uneven outcomes, including cyber risk exposure as services digitize
faster than security capacity improves.
For emerging states, the benchmark suggests a focus on closing mid-layer gaps:
standardizing KPI reporting, investing in skilling and cyber capacity (including shared
SOC services), and adopting interoperability standards for public services. These
measures can accelerate adoption and improve ESG credibility without requiring the
fiscal scale of large subsidies.
5.4 Aspirants: inclusion priority states with infrastructure bottlenecks
Aspirant states are characterized by large inclusion needs and significant potential
returns from digitization, but are constrained by infrastructure and institutional
bottlenecks. Constraints may include slower right-of-way execution, limited high-
quality grid capacity for large facilities, lower density of skilled operations talent, and
weaker local ecosystems for enterprise-grade data center operations. Such constraints
limit the near-term feasibility of large hyperscale clusters, but do not reduce the
urgency of inclusion improvements.
In aspirant states, the most credible near-term pathway is to focus on resilient
connectivity and modular compute—especially edge and regional facilities that
support public services such as telemedicine, education delivery, and e-governance.
ESG integration remains important: modular facilities can be designed with high

efficiency, low water impacts, and verified monitoring, avoiding the lock-in of
inefficient small facilities.
Trust governance is particularly critical in aspirant states because vulnerable users
face higher fraud exposure and may have less capacity to recover from digital harms.
Therefore, inclusion programs should explicitly integrate cyber safety, privacy-by-
design, and grievance redressal mechanisms, ensuring that adoption is durable and
does not regress due to high-profile incidents.
5.5 Special-context: islands, Himalayan states, and North-East constraints
Special-context states and UTs face geography-driven constraints such as difficult
terrain, fragile ecosystems, and higher costs of backhaul and power reliability. In
island and Himalayan regions, climate risk and ecological sensitivity increase the
importance of low-impact design, including minimal land use, reduced water draw,
and robust disaster continuity planning. These conditions require that benchmarking
emphasize adaptive pathways rather than penalize geography.
In special-context regions, the highest near-term value often comes from resilient
edge computing for public services, disaster management, and connectivity assurance.
Hybrid connectivity approaches, including satellite or microwave backhaul where
appropriate, can complement fiber expansion. The benchmark therefore emphasizes
resilience-first design principles and the integration of cyber governance into
emergency operations, where the risk of vulnerabilities increases during crises.
A special-context pathway also benefits from regional shared services: shared SOC
capabilities, shared procurement templates for ESG and cyber requirements, and
regional training programs. These reduce duplication and enable smaller jurisdictions
to achieve governance maturity without bearing the full fixed costs of specialized
institutions and monitoring systems.
6. Theme Deep Dive: Cyber Governance within ESG for Green Data Centers
and Inclusion
6.1 Cyber-energy trade-offs and “secure efficiency”
Cyber controls can create additional compute overhead and storage replication, while
weak cyber design can increase outage risk, data loss, and operational disruptions.
Both outcomes have ESG consequences: increased compute overhead raises energy

Vol-04|Issue-12|December|Year-2024 International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)ISSN: 3049-2343
consumption, and incidents increase resource consumption through emergency
operations, re-provisioning, and service downtime. A “secure efficiency” framing
treats cyber resilience as an efficiency enabler because stable operations reduce waste
and reduce the need for redundant over-provisioning.
Secure efficiency requires baseline controls such as asset inventory, configuration
management, identity and access controls, secure logging, and incident response
rehearsals. These controls align with widely used frameworks such as NIST CSF 2.0,
which structures cyber risk management into functions and practices that can be
adopted incrementally (NIST, 2024). For Indian state data centers and public
workloads, adopting such a framework-like structure improves auditability and
facilitates procurement standardization.
A key implication is that ESG for data centers cannot ignore cyber governance.
Facilities may achieve strong PUE improvements while remaining vulnerable to
incidents that disrupt services and erode trust. Therefore, the benchmark integrates
cyber governance into ESG as a core “G” dimension that shapes inclusion and
resilience outcomes.

data.

and data classification rules. Shared environments reduce fragmentation and increase
the feasibility of implementing consistent cyber controls, monitoring, and audit
processes. This is particularly relevant for small departments and local bodies that
may otherwise procure fragmented, low-quality infrastructure.
A key design principle is proportional sovereignty: sensitive workloads can be
isolated and protected without requiring that all workloads run on fully localized,
bespoke infrastructure. Such proportional design reduces ESG burdens, improves

utilization, and enables consistent governance, aligning with the benchmark’s cross-
layer emphasis on efficiency, trust, and inclusion.
6.3 Standards and interoperability as inclusion multipliers
Interoperability standards reduce transaction costs and enable cross-platform service
delivery. For inclusion, interoperability reduces lock-in and enables portability across
states and providers, which is critical for migrant workers, mobile populations, and
firms operating across jurisdictions. Interoperable digital services also enable easier
scaling of innovations and reduce duplication in platform development across
departments.
For ESG, interoperability supports shared monitoring and reporting, enabling
comparable disclosure across facilities and public sector data centers. Standardized
telemetry and reporting also strengthen cyber resilience by improving visibility and
auditability. In practice, interoperable logging standards, asset inventories, and
configuration baselines can reduce incident response time and enable benchmarking
of governance maturity.
States can institutionalize interoperability through standards playbooks, procurement
templates, and governance councils that coordinate across departments and vendors.
Such institutionalization is a relatively low-capital intervention with high systemic
returns, and it is especially valuable for emerging and aspirant states seeking to raise
adoption outcomes without relying solely on physical infrastructure expansion.
6.4 Resilience engineering: grid, water, climate, and disaster
Resilience engineering integrates energy systems, cooling, and continuity planning. In
many Indian states, climate stress and water scarcity make WUE and water-source
transparency central ESG variables, while grid instability increases reliance on
backup generation with emissions and local air quality implications. Data center
growth therefore requires integrated planning that considers grid upgrades, low-
carbon procurement, and water risk management alongside land facilitation.
Resilient design emphasizes efficiency-first cooling, waste-heat reuse where feasible,
and redundancy designed to minimize over-provisioning. The risk is that resilience is
achieved by adding redundancy in a way that lowers utilization and increases absolute
footprint. A benchmark-driven approach therefore rewards “smart resilience”:

Vol-04|Issue-12|December|Year-2024 International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)ISSN: 3049-2343
redundancy and continuity planning that is paired with utilization management,
efficient equipment, and measurable KPIs.
Cyber resilience is intertwined with physical resilience because disasters often trigger
cyber vulnerabilities during emergency operations. Therefore, resilience planning
must include incident response drills, secure remote access protocols, and continuity
plans for identity and access management, aligning with national reporting
requirements and widely used frameworks.
6.5 Inclusion-by-design with cyber-safe service delivery
Digital inclusion programs can be undermined by fraud, identity abuse, and privacy
violations, particularly for first-time users. Inclusion-by-design therefore requires
secure onboarding, privacy-preserving authentication, clear consent mechanisms, and
grievance redressal aligned with consumer protection. These requirements are not
cosmetic: they shape whether people choose to use digital services and whether
inclusion gains persist over time.
State digital programs that rely on cloud and data center services can incorporate
standardized cyber controls, data minimization principles, and secure-by-default user
interfaces. Procurement can require baseline controls such as encryption, logging,
vulnerability management, and incident response readiness, aligned with national
directions and privacy obligations (CERT-In, 2022; MeitY, 2023). This reduces harm
and builds trust, particularly in low-literacy contexts.
Inclusion-by-design also includes accessibility and language support, which can be
linked to procurement requirements and user testing. When combined with cyber
safety, these measures expand the “effective reach” of digital services beyond raw
connectivity, improving productivity and resilience outcomes—the core outcome
dimensions of the benchmark.
6.6 ESG-integrated cyber metrics and governance
An ESG-integrated cyber approach treats cyber risk as a governance metric with
measurable controls and outcomes, such as time-to-detect, time-to-recover, audit
compliance rates, and the existence of documented playbooks and drills. It also treats
cyber capacity building as a social metric by expanding skilled employment and
improving the reliability of public digital services. This dual framing aligns the “G”
and “S” pillars of ESG with practical infrastructure performance.

7. Methods
7.1 Research design
The study employs a comparative and cross-layer design that combines documentary
analysis, indicator construction, and maturity scoring. The unit of analysis is the
Indian state/UT ecosystem, with national-level context treated as a shared constraint
layer and G20/BRICS archetypes treated as reference models. The method is designed
for replicability and updateability rather than for one-off ranking.
Evidence is triangulated across policy texts, regulator dashboards, mission documents,
and international standards. Where direct quantitative comparability is limited, the
benchmark uses structured ordinal scoring grounded in explicit criteria. This approach
avoids over-claiming precision while enabling decision-relevant comparisons across
states with different reporting maturity.
The design supports two outputs: (i) interpretive maturity clusters that guide pathway
design, and (ii) a quantitative-ordinal hybrid index (G-DIISTI) that can be updated as
new evidence and datasets are published. The index is not a substitute for granular
project appraisal; rather, it is a strategic diagnostic tool.

7.4 The Green Digital Infrastructure Inclusion and Security Transition Index
(G-DIISTI)
The Green Digital Infrastructure Inclusion and Security Transition Index (G-DIISTI)
is designed as a 0–100 readiness and transition measure that integrates eight cross-
layer dimensions. Each dimension is composed of sub-indicators that can be
populated from open sources and documentary evidence. The index is explicitly
designed to be updated, enabling states to track progress over time rather than being
locked into a single-year snapshot.
Dimension weights are selected to reflect the joint importance of physical readiness
and governance-based trust. Infrastructure receives the largest weight because power
reliability and network readiness are binding constraints for data center capacity and
quality of service. Risk and trust governance receives a high weight because cyber
incidents and privacy harms directly reduce adoption and inclusion. Sustainability
outcomes are given a distinct weight so that performance is measured rather than
assumed when infrastructure scales.
The index structure is compatible with both hub states and inclusion-priority states.
Hub states can score highly by demonstrating verified ESG KPIs at scale, while
inclusion-priority states can improve scores through governance capacity building,
cyber-safe inclusion design, and resilient connectivity improvements, even before
hyperscale investment arrives.
7.5 Scoring rubric and evidence protocol
Each sub-indicator is scored on a 0–5 rubric. A score of 0 indicates absence of policy
or capability; 1–2 indicates nascent intent and partial implementation; 3 indicates
operational capability with measurable progress but persistent gaps; 4 indicates

Vol-04|Issue-12|December|Year-2024 International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)ISSN: 3049-2343
advanced implementation with regular monitoring and KPI integration; and 5
indicates best-in-class performance with transparent KPIs, audits, and demonstrated
outcomes. The rubric is designed to minimize false precision while remaining
decision-relevant.
The evidence protocol requires that each score be accompanied by a traceable
evidence note referencing an open-source document or dashboard statement. For
example, a policy score can be evidenced by an official policy notification, while an
incident readiness score can be evidenced by compliance processes aligned with
national directions. Where numeric indicators exist, the normalized value is mapped
to rubric thresholds specified ex ante.
The protocol also includes governance for updating: scores should be refreshed
annually or when major policy changes occur, and evidence notes should retain the
original publication date. This supports transparency and prevents “metric drift”
where scores are updated without traceable justification.

7.7 Reliability, robustness, and sensitivity analysis
Reliability is addressed through rubric consistency checks and evidence triangulation.
For rubric-scored indicators, at least two reviewers or a cross-check mechanism can

Vol-04|Issue-12|December|Year-2024 International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)ISSN: 3049-2343
be used in formal applications to reduce subjective drift. In this report, rubric
application is described transparently, and the illustrative scorecard is explicitly
labeled as illustrative to avoid misAnalysis as an official ranking.
Robustness is evaluated through sensitivity of overall rankings to reasonable weight
changes. For example, weights can be varied by ±20% within each dimension while
preserving the 100-point sum, and results can be checked for stability of broad
clusters rather than exact rank. This prevents over-reliance on a single weight scheme
and reinforces the diagnostic rather than competitive purpose of the benchmark.
The sensitivity approach also supports policy relevance: if a state’s position changes
dramatically under minor weight shifts, the diagnostic conclusion is that the state’s
profile is unbalanced and that policy should prioritize closing gaps rather than
celebrating an overall score. Balanced profiles are more robust, which aligns with
ESG logic that penalizes hidden risks.
