Liquid cooling systems (LCS) have emerged as a highly effective alternative, offering 
superior thermal management capabilities compared with traditional air-based cooling 
approaches. By circulating specialized coolants directly through cold plates, heat 
exchangers, or immersion setups, LCS can efficiently absorb and transfer heat away from 
high-power components, significantly reducing operating temperatures and energy 
consumption. The enhanced heat transfer efficiency of liquid cooling allows data centers 
to achieve higher equipment densities while maintaining system reliability and reducing 
the need for excessive airflow, which in turn lowers fan power consumption and overall 
operational costs. Moreover, liquid cooling systems enable more uniform temperature 
distribution across server racks and minimize the risk of thermal hotspots, which can lead 
to component failure if left unaddressed. 
Despite these advantages, ensuring the long-term stability and reliability of LCS 
remains a critical concern. Several potential failure modes can compromise system 
performance, including coolant leaks, material corrosion, mineral or particulate 
accumulation, flow obstruction, pump or valve malfunctions, and sensor inaccuracies. 
Any of these issues can disrupt thermal management, leading to elevated component 
temperatures, increased energy usage, and potentially shortened equipment lifespans. 
Furthermore, the integration of LCS requires careful consideration of system design, 
coolant chemistry, material compatibility, and maintenance strategies to prevent 
degradation over time. 
Therefore, the successful implementation of liquid cooling systems in modern, high-
density data centers relies on a comprehensive approach that combines robust design, 
proactive monitoring, and effective maintenance protocols. Real-time monitoring 
technologies, predictive diagnostics, and regular system inspections are essential to detect 
early signs of failure and to maintain operational stability. This review provides a 
systematic examination of the technical methods, operational strategies, and management 
practices developed to enhance the reliability of LCS, emphasizing the importance of 
continuous system monitoring, preventive maintenance, and lifecycle management. By 
addressing these aspects, data centers can fully leverage the benefits of liquid cooling 
technologies, achieving improved energy efficiency, system stability, and sustainable 
high-performance operation [1]. 
2. Background of Liquid Cooling Systems 
2.1. Advantages of Liquid Cooling Systems 
Liquid cooling systems have increasingly become the preferred thermal management 
solution in modern data centers due to their superior heat transfer efficiency and energy 
performance compared with conventional air cooling methods. Liquids such as water and 
engineered dielectric coolants possess much higher specific heat capacities and thermal 
conductivities than air, enabling them to absorb and transport larger quantities of heat 
with comparatively lower flow rates [2]. This capacity allows liquid cooling systems to 
handle the rapidly increasing heat loads produced by high-density servers, CPUs, GPUs, 
and memory modules, while reducing reliance on high-speed fans, which can contribute 
to noise, vibration, and additional energy consumption. 
Beyond their fundamental thermal advantages, liquid cooling systems offer multiple 
operational benefits. They allow for more uniform temperature distribution across server 
racks, effectively minimizing hotspots that can reduce component lifespan or lead to 
performance throttling [3]. Liquid cooling also facilitates compact data center layouts, 
permitting higher equipment density without compromising system reliability. This is 
particularly important for high-performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence 
workloads, where power densities per rack can exceed 20 kW. In such scenarios, studies 
indicate that liquid cooling systems can reduce cooling energy consumption by up to 35% 
compared to traditional air cooling approaches, thereby improving the overall Power 
Usage Effectiveness (PUE) of the facility [4]. 

GBP Proceedings Series 
 
 
Vol. 20 (2026) 
42 
 
Additionally, liquid cooling enables diverse deployment strategies, including direct-
to-chip cooling, rear-door heat exchangers, in-row cooling units, and full-immersion 
techniques. These configurations allow data centers to tailor cooling solutions to specific 
workloads and equipment arrangements, improving system flexibility and scalability. 
The precise thermal control provided by liquid cooling also contributes to better hardware 
longevity, reducing the risk of temperature-induced component degradation and 
operational downtime. Together, these advantages make liquid cooling a critical enabler 
of high-performance, energy-efficient, and reliable data center operations [5]. 
2.2. Liquid Cooling in High-Density Environments 
With the continuous growth of AI, HPC, and big data processing workloads, the 
thermal and energy demands of modern data centers are escalating rapidly. High-density 
server configurations, where power densities can exceed 30 kW per rack, place enormous 
stress on traditional air-cooling systems, which often struggle to maintain uniform and 
safe operating temperatures. Liquid cooling addresses these limitations by offering highly 
efficient heat removal directly at the source of heat generation, allowing data centers to 
maintain optimal thermal conditions even under extreme computational loads [6]. 
In high-density environments, liquid cooling provides additional advantages beyond 
basic heat removal. By reducing temperature gradients and stabilizing operational 
conditions, it enhances system reliability and minimizes the risk of thermal-induced 
failures. Compact server layouts become feasible, supporting greater computational 
power per unit area while lowering infrastructure footprint [7]. This capability not only 
reduces physical space requirements but also enables better airflow management, energy 
savings, and operational flexibility. Furthermore, precise thermal regulation offered by 
liquid cooling allows data centers to maintain consistent performance over extended 
periods of high workload operation, which is crucial for mission-critical computing tasks. 
Liquid cooling also supports energy-efficient design strategies, as the reduced need for 
extensive air movement lowers fan power consumption and enables integration with 
renewable energy sources or advanced heat reuse systems. 
Overall, liquid cooling systems have transitioned from being an optional 
enhancement to a strategic necessity in modern high-density data centers. Their superior 
thermal performance, energy efficiency, flexibility in deployment, and contribution to 
hardware longevity make them indispensable for meeting the growing computational 
and energy challenges associated with AI, HPC, and large-scale data analytics 
applications [8]. By enabling higher operational densities, improving energy utilization, 
and maintaining stable thermal conditions, liquid cooling systems play a pivotal role in 
supporting the sustainable and efficient growth of next-generation data center 
infrastructures. 
3. Failure Modes in Liquid Cooling Systems 
Although liquid cooling systems provide superior thermal management compared 
with traditional air cooling, their increased complexity introduces a range of potential 
failure modes that can affect system performance, reliability, and operational safety. 
Understanding these failure modes is critical for developing robust strategies to ensure 
the stability and longevity of these systems [9]. Failure mechanisms in liquid cooling can 
broadly be categorized into leaks, corrosion, clogging, and sensor malfunctions, each of 
which can have significant operational implications if not properly addressed. 
3.1. Leaks 
Leaks represent one of the most serious and immediate threats to liquid cooling 
systems [10]. They can occur at various points in the system, including pipe connections, 
fittings, coolant reservoirs, pumps, and cold plates. Even minor leaks can compromise 
system efficiency, while major leaks may cause catastrophic failures, such as electrical 

GBP Proceedings Series 
 
 
Vol. 20 (2026) 
43 
 
short circuits, hardware damage, or prolonged system downtime [11]. Early detection of 
leaks is therefore essential, and it often requires the integration of dedicated leak detection 
sensors, routine visual inspections, and real-time monitoring of system pressure and flow 
rates. Effective sealing, proper material selection, and careful system assembly are also 
fundamental preventive measures that reduce the likelihood of leak occurrence. 
3.2. Corrosion 
Corrosion is a common degradation process in liquid cooling systems, particularly 
when water-based or chemically reactive coolants are used. Electrochemical reactions 
between the coolant and system materials, such as metals and alloys, can gradually 
deteriorate components, forming oxides or other by-products that impede fluid flow. 
Corrosion not only reduces the efficiency of heat transfer but can also contribute to 
clogging and localized system failures [12]. Preventive strategies include the use of 
corrosion inhibitors in the coolant, selection of corrosion-resistant materials, and careful 
control of pH, dissolved oxygen, and conductivity within the coolant. Regular monitoring 
of coolant chemistry and periodic maintenance are essential for sustaining long-term 
system integrity [13]. 
3.3. Clogging 
Clogging occurs when particulate matter, including dust, microbial biofilms, 
corrosion by-products, or precipitated minerals, accumulates in flow channels, pumps, 
valves, or heat exchangers. This accumulation restricts fluid circulation, reduces heat 
transfer efficiency, increases system pressure, and can place undue stress on pumps and 
other components [14]. Poor coolant quality, inadequate filtration, and insufficient 
maintenance often exacerbate clogging problems [15]. To prevent these issues, data 
centers typically implement filtration systems, periodic flushing, and chemical treatment 
of the coolant to maintain low levels of particulate matter and inhibit microbial growth. 
3.4. Sensor Malfunctions 
Sensors play a critical role in maintaining proper operation of liquid cooling systems 
by monitoring temperature, flow rate, pressure, and other key parameters. 
Malfunctioning sensors, however, can provide inaccurate readings, potentially causing 
inappropriate system responses [16]. For instance, a faulty temperature sensor may trigger 
unnecessary pumping or fail to detect overheating, while inaccurate flow or pressure 
measurements may prevent timely intervention to correct system anomalies. Such failures 
can reduce overall cooling efficiency, accelerate hardware wear, and increase the risk of 
system downtime. Ensuring sensor reliability involves using high-quality sensing devices, 
redundant monitoring systems, regular calibration, and integration of predictive 
diagnostics to identify early signs of sensor drift or failure [17]. 
4. Stability Assurance Methods 
4.1. Water Quality Management 
Water quality management is critical for maintaining the stability of liquid cooling 
systems. The water used as a coolant must meet specific quality standards to prevent 
corrosion, biofilm formation, and clogging. Key parameters to monitor include pH, 
conductivity, ion concentration, and bacteria count. Regular testing and control of these 
parameters help ensure optimal performance of the system [18]. 
4.1.1. Water Quality Standards 
Water quality standards vary depending on the type of coolant used. Primary-side 
coolants, which are often glycol-based, have different water quality requirements 
compared to secondary-side coolants, which are in direct contact with sensitive electronic

Vol. 20 (2026)

components. Table 1 summarizes the water quality standards for both primary and 
secondary-side coolants.

4.2. Leak Prevention Methods 
Leak prevention is crucial for maintaining system stability. Several strategies are 
employed, including the use of multi-layered sealing designs, leak detection systems, and 
regular inspections. 
4.2.1. Leak Detection Systems 
Leak detection systems are vital in identifying leaks early before they cause serious 
damage. As summarized in Table 2, these systems primarily include conductive sensor 
lines, visual inspection systems, and pressure-based sensors.

4.3. Real-Time Monitoring and Control 
Real-time monitoring is essential for ensuring the proper functioning of liquid 
cooling systems. By continuously monitoring parameters such as temperature, pressure, 
and coolant flow, operators can detect potential issues early and prevent system failures. 
4.3.1. Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU) 
The Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU) plays a critical role in real-time monitoring, 
ensuring the system operates efficiently. As shown in Table 3, it controls coolant flow, 
measures temperature, and helps maintain system stability.

5. Verification of Stability Assurance Methods 
To ensure the effectiveness of stability assurance methods for liquid cooling systems, 
verification through both experimental validation and case studies is crucial. These 
methods allow for confirmation of the reliability and operational performance of cooling 
systems under various conditions [19]. The validation process includes testing the 
system's response to variable operating conditions such as changes in coolant temperature, 
flow rates, and external factors like humidity. Experimental validation and case studies 
also help assess the longevity of water quality management, leak prevention methods, 
and real-time monitoring solutions. 
5.1. Experimental Validation 
Experimental validation involves testing liquid cooling systems in controlled 
environments to evaluate their performance, particularly focusing on the effectiveness of 
water quality management, leak prevention, and real-time monitoring. During the 
validation process, data is collected over extended periods to ensure the system's stability 
across various operational conditions. Below are key aspects of experimental validation: 
1. **Water Quality Management Validation**: Water quality is a key factor in ensuring the 
long-term stability of liquid cooling systems [20]. A study conducted by Smith et al. (2021) 
on a high-density data center's liquid cooling system showed that using corrosion 
inhibitors, along with routine pH and conductivity checks, significantly reduced the rate 
of cooling system failures due to corrosion. After implementing optimal water quality 
control, the failure rate of the cooling system was reduced by up to 45%. The study found 
that systems with corrosion inhibitors showed no significant degradation over 12 months, 
while systems without inhibitors saw up to 30% degradation in thermal efficiency during 
the same period. 
2. **Leak Prevention Method Validation**: A field test conducted in a large-scale data 
center with a liquid cooling system equipped with advanced leak detection systems 
showed a 60% reduction in unplanned maintenance. This reduction was attributed to 
early-stage leak detection, which enabled timely repair before leaks led to coolant loss or 
equipment damage. The test monitored the impact of real-time leak detection sensors and 
multi-layered sealing technologies. The results confirmed that early leak detection 
systems could reduce downtime and maintenance costs by up to $200,000 per year, 
compared to traditional leak prevention methods. 
3. **Real-Time Monitoring Systems Validation**: Real-time monitoring technologies 
have become increasingly important in maintaining the stability of liquid cooling systems. 
In a comparative study performed by Zhang et al. (2020), real-time monitoring systems 
incorporating temperature, pressure, and flow sensors were installed in a sample liquid 
cooling system. Over a 6-month period, the system with real-time monitoring maintained 
an optimal thermal environment in servers, with a cooling efficiency improvement of 20%, 
while the non-monitored system saw a decline in cooling efficiency by 10% due to 
overheating in certain servers. The findings indicated that integrating real-time 
monitoring significantly improved both the efficiency and reliability of the cooling 
systems. 
5.2. Case Studies 
In addition to experimental validation, case studies provide real-world insights into 
the effectiveness of stability assurance methods. The following case studies demonstrate 

GBP Proceedings Series 
 
 
Vol. 20 (2026) 
46 
 
how verification methods have been implemented and their impact on system 
performance. 
1. **Case Study: Large Data Center in Silicon Valley** A data center in Silicon Valley 
implemented a comprehensive liquid cooling system that included a multi-layered 
approach to water quality management, leak detection, and real-time monitoring. Over 
the course of two years, the data center experienced a dramatic reduction in maintenance-
related downtime (by 50%) and cooling-related failures (by 35%). The case study also 
highlighted the significant role of predictive maintenance enabled by real-time 
monitoring data. The system's performance showed a 25% improvement in PUE (Power 
Usage Effectiveness), which translates to a considerable reduction in operational costs for 
cooling. 
2. **Case Study: European High-Density Data Center**A high-density data center in 
Europe, known for hosting AI and machine learning operations, deployed an advanced 
leak detection system using conductive sensor lines and a flow-meter-based monitoring 
network. After six months, leakage rates were reduced by 60%, and the system showed 
enhanced performance in preventing coolant loss during high-demand periods. The 
installation of dual-redundant pumps and cooling plates helped reduce system failure 
rates, and operational efficiency increased by 18%. Furthermore, the cooling system's 
effective capacity was enhanced, enabling it to support additional IT load without 
additional energy costs. 
6. Conclusion 
In summary, liquid cooling systems play an increasingly critical role in managing the 
growing heat output of modern data centers, particularly as computational densities and 
energy consumption continue to rise. Their superior thermal management capabilities 
allow for higher server densities, improved energy efficiency, and enhanced operational 
reliability compared with traditional air cooling methods. However, the complex nature 
of these systems introduces potential risks, including leaks, corrosion, clogging, and 
sensor malfunctions, which must be carefully addressed to maintain stable and safe 
operation. 
Ensuring the long-term stability and reliability of liquid cooling systems requires a 
comprehensive approach that integrates effective water quality management, corrosion 
prevention, filtration, leak detection, and real-time monitoring technologies. Predictive 
maintenance strategies, combined with advanced sensors and intelligent diagnostic tools, 
can identify early signs of system degradation, allowing for timely intervention before 
failures occur. In addition, proper material selection, routine system inspections, and 
adherence to operational best practices are essential components of a robust liquid cooling 
management framework. 
Looking forward, the continued development of advanced monitoring technologies, 
automated leak detection systems, and smart predictive maintenance approaches will 
further enhance the performance, safety, and reliability of liquid cooling systems. As data 
centers evolve to support increasingly demanding workloads, these technologies will be 
essential for achieving sustainable, high-density, and energy-efficient operations, 
ensuring that liquid cooling systems can meet the future requirements of next-generation 
computing infrastructure. By combining technological innovation with proactive system 
management, liquid cooling systems can provide the stable and efficient thermal 
environment necessary for long-term data center operation.

Current Status and Challenges for
Liquid-Cooled Data Centers
Hongwei Chen and Dong Li*
School of Energy and Mechanical Engineering, Nanjing Normal University, Nanjing, China
Keywords: data center, liquid cooling, immersion, cold plate, spray
1 INTRODUCTION
Data centers (DCs) are computing structures housing a large number of information and
communications
technology
devices
installed
for
processing,
storing,
and
transmitting
information (Khalaj and Halgamuge, 2017). In recent years, the size and number of DCs have
been growing dramatically (Zhang, et al., 2018). According to statistics, as of the end of 2017, there
were 285,000 DCs in use in China, and the equipment in DCs consumed more than 120 billion kWh
of electricity annually, accounting for 2% of China’s total electricity consumption. Based on this
trend, it is predicted that by 2022, China’s DCs will consume more than 250 billion kWh of electricity
(Gong et al., 2022). Cooling systems consume 30–50% of the total DC energy consumption (Zhang
et al., 2014), and failure to reduce cooling system energy consumption will undoubtedly result in a
huge energy waste for the growing DC demand.
In the meantime, with the rapid development of new high-performance chips, the heat ﬂux of the
servers is increasing. If the heat of the servers cannot be released in time, the computing efﬁciency
and stability of the chip will be affected and even cause the failure of electronic equipment (Murshed
and Castro, 2017). Traditional air cooling can no longer meet the cooling needs of DCs; thus, it is
necessary to adopt efﬁcient cooling technology to ensure the safe operation of electronic equipment.
Liquid cooling technology uses liquid as a refrigerant to transfer heat through direct or indirect
contact with the heating element. Compared with air, the volumetric heat capacity of water is about
3500 times higher and the thermal conductivity is 25 times higher (Zimmermann et al., 2012), so for
high-density servers, liquid cooling has become the obvious choice for DCs.
2 Current Research Status of Liquid-Cooled DCs
2.1 Classiﬁcation of Liquid Cooling Technology
At present, the liquid cooling technology for the servers in DCs mainly includes immersion liquid
cooling, cold plate liquid cooling, and spray liquid cooling. The difference lies mainly in the different
ways of heat dissipation. Immersion liquid cooling is to completely soak the server in the cooling
liquid and take away the heat of the heating element by single- or two-phase cooling. The cold plate
liquid cooling is to connect the liquid cooling plate with the high-power heating element of the
server, and other low-power heating elements are assisted by air cooling to achieve the overall cooling
of the server. The spray liquid cooling is used to spray the cooling liquid on the surface of the heating
element for heat dissipation. There are three main types of liquid cooling solutions that are discussed
in the following subsections.
2.1.1 Immersion Liquid Cooling
According to whether the coolant undergoes phase change, the immersion liquid cooling is generally
divided into single- and two-phase immersion liquid cooling. As shown in Figure 1A for single-
phase immersion liquid cooling, the low-temperature coolant is sent to the heat exchanger by the
circulation pump after absorbing the heat from the heating elements of the server using sensible heat.
Then, it re-enters the liquid cooling tank to cool the server when the coolant is cooled by warm water

in the heat exchanger. Coolant control is relatively simple in
single-phase liquid cooling, and coolant loss is low with good
sealing, thereby eliminating the demand for frequent coolant
replenishment. In the two-phase immersion liquid cooling
system, the server is immersed in a liquid cooling tank
containing low-boiling-point cooling liquid. As shown in
Figure 1B, when the ambient heat reaches certain conditions,
the cooling liquid will use latent heat to absorb the heat and
produce a boiling phase change to cool down the equipment. The
cooling liquid vapor is condensed by the condenser tube to the
liquid state and then returned to the liquid cooling tank (Xie et al.,
2022).
2.1.2 Cold Plate Liquid Cooling
Generally speaking, the cold plate liquid cooling mostly solves
the heat dissipation of the devices with high heat generation in
the server, such as the central processing unit (CPU), while
other devices with low heat generation, such as hard disks and
main memory, still rely on air cooling. The cold plate liquid
cooling mainly transfers the heat from the heating element of
the server to the circulating coolant indirectly through the
liquid cooling plate. The circulation process is shown in
Figure 1C. First, a manifold is arranged on the liquid
cooling cabinet to convey the coolant to each liquid cooling
computing node. Second, the inlet and outlet are connected
with quick connectors, and the main connector is connected to
the built-in or external coolant distribution unit (CDU). Third,
the CDU is connected with the outdoor cooling unit, thus
completing the liquid cooling cycle of the whole cabinet.
Compared
with
traditional
air-cooled
servers,
this
technology signiﬁcantly improves the
energy utilization
efﬁciency of DCs, with lower noise, and the installation and
maintenance are basically the same as that of air-cooled servers
(Kheirabadi and Groulx, 2016).
2.1.3 Spray Liquid Cooling
Spray liquid cooling is a liquid cooling technology in which the
server is modiﬁed to deploy the corresponding spray device, and
the coolant is directly sprayed on the surface of the heating
element through the nozzle to absorb heat and is then
discharged. Because it is a targeted cooling technology,
compared with immersion liquid cooling, the required dose
of coolant is lower, and the implementation is more economical.
As shown in Figure 1D, the sprayed liquid cooling system
mainly includes a liquid cooling cabinet, heat exchanger,
circulation pump, and outdoor cooling unit. The liquid
cooling cabinet is connected to the heat exchanger through
piping, i.e., the heat of the heat-generating components of the
server in the cabinet is absorbed by the coolant and cooled down
in the heat exchanger. Sprayed liquid cooling has the features of
high device integration, high energy efﬁciency, and low noise.
Compared with air-cooled DCs, the total energy consumption
of sprayed liquid-cooled DCs can be reduced by 25.8%
(Kandasamy et al., 2022).

plate liquid cooling, and (D) spray liquid cooling.

July 2022 | Volume 10 | Article 952680
2
Chen and Li
Liquid-Cooled Data Centers

2.2 Application of Liquid Cooling
Technology
Among the three liquid cooling methods, cold plate liquid
cooling is the most widely used. In the cold plate liquid
cooling system, the CDU plays a crucial role, not only by
providing circulating coolant for the system but also by
transporting heat from the cabinet cooling system to the
outdoor cooling unit, and the temperature of the coolant can
be ﬂexibly regulated to meet different cooling requirements.
Since CDU failure may lead to liquid cooling system paralysis,
the equipment in CDU should be considered for redundant
setup, and the circulating pump as the core component is
generally used for one use and one standby. The current
research on cold plate liquid cooling focuses on strengthening
the heat transfer technology and designing efﬁcient micro-
channel
heat
sinks
for
heat-generating
components
(Kheirabadi and Groulx., 2016). There have been many
application cases of cold plate liquid cooling. For example,
IBM Power 575 and 775 supercomputers, using liquid-cooled
cold plates connected directly to the processor and air-cooled
auxiliary components, have achieved better energy-saving effect
(Ellsworth et al., 2012). In addition, Beijing water-cooled
supercomputing center uses a room temperature water cooling
technology to solve the memory cooling problem of the DC,
which reduces the DC energy consumption and makes it reach
the highest energy-saving level (Wang et al., 2021). Furthermore,
the all-liquid cooling solution from Huawei, which uses liquid
technology, has better realized the high-density deployment of
information technology (IT) equipment and improved the
energy use efﬁciency of DCs (Wang et al., 2019), etc.
Immersion liquid cooling not only has high heat transfer
efﬁciency but also avoids local hot spots. It is currently the
most effective technical means to solve the problem of high-
performance server heating, which can increase the power of a
single cabinet to 100 kW or even more than 200 kW. Research on
immersion systems is observed to be growing in the 21st century.
In 2009, Green Revolution Cooling rebooted the concept of open
bath immersion cooling by bringing commercial bath immersion
systems to the high-performance computing industry. Moreover,
the Open Compute Project ofﬁcially embraced a new project
under the Rack & Power as part of Advanced Cooling Solutions in
2018,
while
the
ﬁrst
documented
industry
standard
for
immersion systems was presented at the Open Compute
Project
summit
in
San
Jose
in
2019.
Midas
Green
Technologies designed and built the ﬁrst immersive DC
during the same year (Pambudi et al., 2022). In China, Sugon
has launched an immersion cooling server, which can reduce the
power usage effectiveness (PUE) of the DC room to 1.05 and
reduce energy consumption by more than 30% compared to
traditional air-cooled DC. In addition, Alibaba’s “Kirin” server
does not require air conditioning, fans, or other accessories, and it
can be deployed anywhere on the ground, thereby saving more
than 75% of space. In the research on cooling media, the U.S.
company 3M has developed a coolant called Novec, which has a
lower boiling point than pure water, ﬂuorinated liquid, and
mineral oil (Zhao et al., 2021).
Nozzle design is the key issue in the design of spray liquid
cooling system, as the nozzle manufacturing process and nozzle
structure affect the spray parameters and cooling performance
(Chen et al., 2022). The heat transfer mechanism in the spray
cooling process is more complex, while the theoretical basis of
the research is relatively small and is still at the laboratory stage.
Kandasamy et al. developed a lab-scale spray-cooled rack with
PF5060 coolant using phase change heat transfer, which can
make the temperature distribution on key components such as
CPU and graphics processing unit more uniform compared
with the cold plate liquid cooling method, and the total energy
consumption of spray-cooled DCs is reduced by 25.8%
compared with air-cooled DCs (Kandasamy et al., 2022).
Due to the limited application scenarios of sprayed liquid
cooling technology, only a small number of DCs have
adopted this technology, such as the Shanghai Big Data
Proving
Ground,
which
uses
modular
containerized
technology and is combined with sprayed liquid cooling
technology to achieve an IT load of 284 kW and control the
PUE of IT equipment within a stable range, which not only
reduces the cost of building a DC but also improves the energy
utilization efﬁciency of the DC. Spray cooling has great
potential for application in DCs and thus merits further
research
to
optimize
its
cooling
performance
for
its
application prospects (Wang et al., 2021).
3 OPPORTUNITIES AND CHALLENGES
At present, DC liquid cooling technology is still in the
preliminary
development
stage,
and
it
still
faces
many
problems and challenges. The following points illustrate the
development direction of future DC liquid cooling technology
application research:
1) Because cold plate liquid cooling has lower requirements for
the transformation and adaptation of traditional air-cooled
servers, the technology is relatively mature and will represent
the mainstream of liquid cooling development in the next few
years. Immersion liquid cooling is currently only applicable to
new DCs due to its special heat dissipation method, while
spray liquid cooling systems are more complex and have the
risk of coolant evaporating and escaping, and still need long-
term research at the laboratory stage.
2) Liquid-cooled DCs use higher temperature coolants, which
makes heat recovery possible for liquid-cooled systems. The
coupling of liquid cooling technology and heat recovery will
further improve the energy utilization efﬁciency of DCs,
which can achieve broader energy saving and emission
reduction
by
using
waste
heat
for
district
heating,
providing domestic hot water, etc.
3) In the cold plate liquid cooling system, there is often an
uneven distribution of the ﬂow of individual servers in a single
cabinet, which may lead to local hot spots or wasted energy
consumption of individual servers; thus, it is also crucial to
study the ﬂow characteristics and optimal design research of
each parallel branch pipeline of servers.

4 CONCLUSION
The application of liquid cooling technology has greatly reduced the
energy consumption of DCs, which is an important way to improve
the energy efﬁciency of DCs and one of the future development trends.
This study introduced the cooling methods and system components of
three liquid cooling technologies and brieﬂy analyzed their
applications, pointing out the development direction of liquid
cooling technology application research. In the future, the industry
should actively pay attention to the changes in liquid cooling
technology,
actively
promote
its
development,
and
lay
the
foundation for the realization of high-performance DC construction.

Abstract
Modern data centers are facing unprecedented pressure. Artificial Intelligence (AI), 
high-performance computing, edge systems, and compact servers are increasing 
energy consumption and generating more heat. Conventional cooling methods 
cannot meet these demands. As rack densities have increased from 5 to 10 kW 
per rack to 30, 50, or even 100 kW, the way thermal management is handled has 
changed completely. Liquid cooling has become one of the most practical and 
scalable ways to meet these problems. What was once considered a niche or 
experimental solution is now widely adopted by hyperscale’s, colocation providers, 
and enterprise data centers worldwide. This evolution is closely linked to the rapid 
expansion of mobile networks and Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystems, where edge 
data centers play a critical role in supporting latency-sensitive and data-intensive 
applications. As a result, efficient thermal management has become essential to 
ensure reliability and scalability in these distributed computing environments. The 
main objective of this study is to apply Neural Networks (NN) based on a cluster of 
metrics derived from the analysis of immersion cooling and direct chip cooling. These 
are used to analyze these metrics using a technique called a Multilayer Perceptron 
(MLP) and Radial Basis Function (RBF), which can yield one or more dependent 
variables to address the problems of energy usage and thermal output. A synthetic 
thermo-hydraulic dataset was generated to simulate operational cooling scenarios 
associated with liquid-to-air and liquid-to-liquid architectures in AI-oriented data 
centers. The simulation-driven dataset enabled the evaluation of multiple thermal 
and flow-related metrics under varying workload conditions using MLP and RBF 
neural-network models. The simulation results reveal that thermal and cooling-related 
variables—particularly ΔT, airflow, and mass flow—consistently have the strongest 
influence on system performance, regardless of model configuration. This finding 
highlights that efficient heat-dissipation mechanisms primarily drive system stability 
and energy efficiency. It supports the scalability and effectiveness of liquid-cooling 
solutions under high thermal loads.

Page 2 of 24
Cortés Discover Networks            (2026) 2:33 
1  Introduction
As AI workloads push the limits of thermal design, data center cooling is undergoing a 
historic acceleration. And now, new research from DCF (Dielectric Cooling Fluid) and 
Endeavor Business Intelligence, commissioned by CoolIT Systems, Ecolab, and Xylem, 
shows how operators are adapting their infrastructure to rising rack densities, liquid-
cooling requirements, and the realities of direct-to-chip single-phase, two-phase, and 
immersion-cooling adoption.
This paper presents key developments in data center cooling system technologies and 
explores the simulation of metrics for improving next-generation cooling infrastruc­
ture. The study adopts the AI to facilitate the design and testing of Neural Networks 
(NN). These networks are provided with independent variables, which are processed 
through hidden layers containing a specified number of elements, to generate one or 
more dependent variables. This approach grants the identification of the most satisfac­
tory metrics within a given scenario.
Similarly, we must consider rack power density in both general-purpose and advanced-
performance applications. In the first, we must consider everything related to Central 
Processing Units (CPUs), email, web servers, and business applications, while the sec­
ond relates to high-performance computing and workloads (Graphics Processing Units 
(GPUs), AI training, modeling). In Fig. 1, we observe the rack densities in both contexts, 
indicating some latency.
In Fig. 1, we see a range of rack densities from more than 30 kW down to 10 kW, and a 
smaller range of 5 kW. Therefore, high-performance computing and AI workloads peak 
at 44 kW, while general-purpose workloads peak at 39 kW. But we must keep in mind 
that there are companies, for example, Blackwell, that consume 120 kW. So, as we can 
see, a small percentage approaches this figure. This really reflects the cooling needs we 
will have in the future and the problems that will emerge as densities increase so rapidly.
Similarly, the percentage and implementations of AI that use liquid cooling must 
be considered. In Fig. 2, between 40 and 59% of their AI implementations were liquid 
cooled. While this is the trend, it’s important to note that some AI implementations are 
still air cooled.
As we mentioned before, there are companies whose thermal density exceeds 30 kW, 
reaching 120 kW or more, for example, 160 kW. Given these situations, liquid cooling is 
the most viable option for cooling the racks, as no other implementation is available for 
this purpose. Similarly, there is infrastructure in the racks that has implemented many 
chips, which can be air cooled. This indicates that we can implement racks that consume 
80 kW per rack with liquid cooling and 120 kW or more with air cooling.
In Fig. 2, there is a 50% difference in performance between air cooling and liquid cool­
ing for the final generation of AI racks that could be air cooled.
Certainly, with liquid cooling, having 16 kW per rack for general-purpose comput­
ing is quite normal. But at the same time, if you consider the projections for CPUs and 
general-purpose computing, the densities may not reach, as at the rack level, the same 
120 kW racks, but at the chip and server level, there are good arguments for requiring 
Keywords  Artificial intelligent, Data centers, Cooling methods, Metrics, Neural 
networks, Multilayer perceptron, Radial Basis function, Synthetic datasets

Page 3 of 24
Cortés Discover Networks            (2026) 2:33 
liquid cooling, at least in a hybrid form, to manage some of the hottest CPUs and GPUs. 
Some hyperscale customers use hybrid designs.
So, it’s worth considering the reasons behind the AI implementations; some of them 
are liquid cooled. Obviously, this is being planned for both the present and the future. As 
workloads continue to increase, they become denser and more challenging, thus requir­
ing more liquid cooling. And, in fact, we’ll need another cooling topology to come into 
play: two-stage immersion. And with respect to the chips themselves, they generate hot 
spots that require liquid cooling, especially on general-purpose CPUs, prompting the 
industry to rush to overcome the challenge.
Fig. 2  The percentage and implementations of AI that use liquid cooling
 
Fig. 1  Density of rack in general purpose workload versus high performance computing and AI workloads
 

Page 4 of 24
Cortés Discover Networks            (2026) 2:33 
The dataset used to generate Figs. 1 and 2 corresponds to a synthetic dataset specifi­
cally designed to simulate thermal-density and cooling-adoption trends in modern AI-
oriented data centers. The synthetic observations (n = 100) were generated based on 
representative ranges reported in prior literature, industrial technical reports, hyperscale 
infrastructure documentation, and publicly available data related to rack power density 
and liquid-cooling adoption. The dataset was created to support exploratory analysis and 
comparative visualization of cooling trends under increasing AI and High-Performance 
Computing (HPC) workloads. The use of synthetic datasets in this context enables con­
trolled evaluation of thermo-hydraulic behavior under multiple operational scenarios 
that would be difficult to reproduce consistently in production-scale data centers. Syn­
thetic data generation also facilitates scalability analysis, parameter sensitivity evalua­
tion, and neural-network training under varying workload conditions. Furthermore, 
this approach aligns with emerging research trends in Generative AI, where advanced 
generative architectures, including diffusion models and transformer-based systems, are 
increasingly employed to create realistic synthetic datasets for predictive infrastructure 
optimization and intelligent thermal-management applications. After generation, the 
data were curated, normalized, and processed in Microsoft Excel for graphical represen­
tation. Therefore, the figures should be interpreted as synthetic trend-oriented simula­
tions rather than direct measurements obtained from a physical experimental platform. 
The complete dataset and graph-generation resources are publicly available in the asso­
ciated GitHub repository, available at: ​h​t​t​p​s​:​/​/​g​i​t​h​u​b​.​c​o​m​/​a​c​o​r​t​e​s​c​a​s​t​i​l​l​o​/​D​a​t​a​s​e​t​-​l​i​q​u​i​d​
-​t​o​-​a​i​r​-​c​o​o​l​i​n​g​-​a​n​d​-​l​i​q​u​i​d​-​t​o​-​a​i​r​-​P​e​r​f​o​r​m​a​n​c​e​.​
However, the interesting thing is that we are seeing a disparity between the needs of 
continuous CPU workloads, i.e., traditional cooling, and liquid cooling.
The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:
 	•
First, this work comprehensively characterizes the key thermal challenges of 
integrating liquid and air cooling in high-density racks, with a focus on AI workloads.
 	•
Next, it introduces a specialized metric framework for Multi-Layer Perceptron 
(MLP) neural networks to precisely monitor hybrid cooling performance.
 	•
Additionally, the study presents a scalable data center network architecture 
optimized for high-fidelity thermal simulations.
 	•
Finally, it proposes a simulation and optimization approach using interdependent 
variables to identify peak cooling efficiency and reduce thermal bottlenecks in 
modern data centers.
In this article, we apply machine learning with neural networks to a set of metrics ini­
tially focused on air cooling and later liquid cooling, with the goal of meeting increasing 
rack level workloads and serving a diverse set of customers. Multilayer perceptron algo­
rithms are used in simulations to obtain normalized results of the independent variables 
introduced into the pattern, after selecting the metrics and labeling them with their 
respective names and numerical values.
Modern data centers must address the growing demand for low-latency processing, 
high data throughput, and continuous availability, driven by the rapid expansion of 5G, 
6G, and IoT devices. Higher computational densities lead to increased thermal stress, 
making effective thermal management—such as liquid cooling—crucial for maintaining 
system stability and scalability.

Page 5 of 24
Cortés Discover Networks            (2026) 2:33 
The acquisition of large-scale real-world thermal datasets from operational AI-ori­
ented data centers remains technically challenging due to infrastructure restrictions, 
operational sensitivity, cost, and limited public availability. Consequently, synthetic data­
sets and simulation-driven approaches have become increasingly relevant for evaluat­
ing cooling strategies, validating predictive models, and supporting the development of 
intelligent thermal-management systems. Recent advances in Generative Artificial Intel­
ligence further suggest that synthetic thermal data generation may become an essential 
component for scalable optimization, anomaly detection, and autonomous infrastruc­
ture management in next-generation data centers.
This report is divided into the following sections: Section 2, relatedwork; Section 3, 
Materials and Methods; Section 4, Discussion, analysis of the data experimentation 
results; and Section 5, conclusions andrecommendations for additional research.
2  Related work
Recent research has shifted from air-cooling to high-efficiency liquid-cooling to manage 
rising rack thermal densities—heat generated by densely packed servers. The guidelines 
in [1] and the industrial roadmaps in [3] establish foundational infrastructure. Next, the 
literature addresses external sectors and data center scalability. Some studies address 
thermal management in electric vehicle batteries [2], but most focus on data centers. For 
example, simulations of free cooling—using outside air or water instead of mechanical 
chillers—integrated with liquid models, assess performance in high-temperature envi­
ronments [4]. Studies on supercomputing clusters, such as HAWK, analyze how varia­
tions in water supply temperature impact performance [5].
The growth of mobile networks and IoT systems now overloads data centers with traf­
fic and computational demand. The rise of 5G devices, edge computing, and latency-
sensitive applications has increased rack power densities and nonstop workloads, 
intensifying thermal stress. Efficient cooling is therefore essential for system reliability 
and consistent performance. Liquid cooling technologies have emerged as scalable solu­
tions, making the analysis of cooling performance metrics critical for data centers sup­
porting next-generation mobile and IoT infrastructure.
Advanced hybrid architectures now drive progress in this field. For example, research 
in [6, 9] examines direct-to-chip cooling. In this method, coolant flows directly over pro­
cessors. Microchannel-based cooling is also used, where tiny liquid channels remove 
heat. Both methods act as exchange interfaces to boost OCP server thermal perfor­
mance. Reference [9] shows that adding heat-dissipation fins and fan-assisted liquid cir­
cuits reliably improves server performance under heavy workloads.
Recent trends also favor intelligent control and mechanical innovations. For instance, 
reference [7] proposes a deep reinforcement learning framework for energy-saving man­
agement. Reference [8] presents an integrated mechanical refrigeration and loop ther­
mosiphon (IMLS), a system combining mechanical chillers with passive loop systems 
for adaptive refrigerant load control. Integrating energy management with cooling tech­
niques is essential for maximizing facility efficiency [10].

they provide, including aspects related to liquid cooling techniques, metrics (thermal 
performance), and areas of use.

3  Materials and methods
This section addresses aspects of liquid-to-air and liquid-to-liquid cooling, examines the 
types and applications of cooling distribution units (CDUs), identifies relevant metrics 
for both cooling methods, and proposes an experimental and analytical model to evalu­
ate these metrics within high-density data centers.
3.1  Direct to chip cooling
Direct-to-chip cooling (D2C) has arisen as a high-efficiency thermal management strat­
egy to address the increasing power densities of modern CPUs and GPUs deployed in 
hyperscale and AI-oriented data centers, as shown Fig. 3. Unlike conventional air-cooling 
systems, D2C technology circulates a dielectric or water-based coolant directly through 
cold plates mounted on high-heat-flux components, allowing localized heat extrac­
tion at the source. This strategy markedly increases heat transfer coefficients, reduces 
thermal resistance, and allows for higher rack power densities while continuing stable 
junction temperatures. Experimental and simulation studies have reported considerable 
increases in energy efficiency, including lower Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) values 
and reduced fan energy consumption. Furthermore, D2C enables heat reuse strategies 
through elevated coolant outlet temperatures, therewith aiding sustainable data center 
design. Consequently, direct-to-chip cooling is a scalable, energy-efficient solution for 
next-gen high-performance computing (HPC) and AI infrastructures.
Given these new cooling technologies, we must consider that the rapid expansion of 
data centers is driving increased demand for cooling solutions. It is worth asking: What 
are the real challenges in meeting those needs? The crux lies in the supply chain, making 
sure there is enough product available and that it can be delivered anywhere, at any time 
it is needed.

3.2  Immersion cooling
Immersion cooling has emerged as an innovative thermal management strategy for high-
density computing infrastructures, particularly in High-Performance Computing (HPC) 
and artificial intelligence workloads, as shown in Fig. 3. From a thermo–fluid dynamic 
perspective, this technology substantially reduces the overall thermal resistance of the 
system by eliminating multiple solid–air interfaces inherent to conventional air-cooling 
architectures. In single-phase configurations, heat generated by electronic components 
is transferred to a dielectric fluid through natural or forced convection, depending on 
the hydraulic design. In contrast, two-phase systems primarily rely on nucleate boiling 
as the dominant heat transfer mechanism, followed by vapor condensation in second­
ary heat exchangers, thereby substantially increasing the overall heat transfer coeffi­
cient. These mechanisms enable rack power densities of 100–150 kW while maintaining 
lower thermal differences and better spatial temperature uniformity. Furthermore, the 
high volumetric heat capacity and chemical stability of dielectric fluids contribute to 
enhanced energy efficiency at the facility level, often reflected in lower Power Usage 
Effectiveness (PUE) values and reduced dependence on conventional Heating, Ventila­
tion, and Air Conditioning (HVAC)  systems. In this context, companies such as Sub­
mer and Green Revolution Cooling have developed modular architectures that integrate 
heat recovery and hydraulic optimization, thereby consolidating immersion cooling as 
a technically robust and expandable approach for future-generation sustainable digital 
frameworks.
3.3  Types and applications for Cooling Distribution Units (CDUs)
Cooling Distribution Units (CDUs) serve as the thermal interface between facility-level 
heat-rejection systems and rack-level liquid-cooling loops in modern data centers. They 
are typically classified into liquid-to-liquid and liquid-to-air configurations. Liquid-to-
liquid CDUs use plate or shell-and-tube heat exchangers to transfer heat to a secondary 
facility water loop, ensuring hydraulic decoupling and precise temperature control. Liq­
uid-to-air CDUs, by contrast, dissipate heat directly to ambient air and are commonly 
deployed in edge or retrofitted environments. CDUs may also be centralized, in-row, 
or rack-mounted, depending on power density and redundancy requirements. Within 
high-density HPC and AI deployments, they support rack loads of 80–150 kW while 
continuing stable flow and supply temperatures. Advanced modular solutions from 
companies such as Vertiv and Schneider Electric integrate variable-speed pumps, intel­
ligent control systems, and live monitoring to increase scalability, functional reliability, 
and overall energy efficiency in liquid-cooled data centers.
A synthetic dataset composed of 100 simulated operational instances was generated to 
evaluate cooling distribution units (CDUs), CDU types, and cooling distribution strat­
egies under air, liquid, and hybrid cooling scenarios. The synthetic observations were 
created using representative parameter ranges obtained from prior literature, vendor 
technical documentation, and publicly available industry reports related to thermal 
management in AI-oriented data centers. The resulting dataset was subsequently pro­
cessed and visualized to generate the bar plots shown in Fig. 4a-b-c.

performance in high-density data centers, future research could significantly extend this 
framework through the integration of advanced Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen­
erative AI) architectures.
Transformer-based models represent a promising direction for modeling dynamic 
thermal behavior in AI-oriented infrastructures [14]. Unlike traditional feedforward 
neural networks, Transformers employ self-attention mechanisms capable of capturing 
long-range dependencies among workload fluctuations, rack-level thermal variations, 
cooling demand, and energy consumption patterns. This capability could improve pre­
dictive thermal management in environments characterized by highly variable work­
loads generated by 5G/6G services, edge computing, and large-scale IoT ecosystems. 
Furthermore, temporal forecasting using Transformers may facilitate proactive cooling 
orchestration [14] and intelligent workload migration strategies in hyperscale data cen­
ters [18].
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) also present important opportunities for 
extending the proposed framework. CNN-based architectures could be employed to 
analyze multidimensional thermal maps, infrared rack images, airflow distributions, and 
localized hotspot formation inside dense computing infrastructures [15]. Through spa­
tial feature extraction, CNNs may support real-time thermal anomaly detection, thermal 
anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, and adaptive rack-level cooling optimiza­
tion [16]. Such capabilities are especially relevant in heterogeneous AI clusters where 
thermal imbalance can significantly affect system reliability and operational efficiency.
In addition, Diffusion Models and other generative frameworks may play a particu­
larly important role in future thermal-management research because they enable the 
generation of high-dimensional synthetic thermo-hydraulic datasets that preserve real­
istic operational distributions. Such approaches are especially valuable in data center 
environments where real-world telemetry data are difficult to obtain due to security, 
operational, or commercial constraints. Synthetic thermal data generated through diffu­
sion-based architectures could support large-scale simulation, neural-network pretrain­
ing, anomaly detection, and stress-testing under extreme AI workload conditions.
The convergence of liquid-cooling infrastructures with Generative AI techniques may 
ultimately lead to fully autonomous thermal-management ecosystems [17] capable of 
self-adaptive optimization. Such systems could dynamically regulate coolant flow, air­
flow distribution, pump speed, and thermal load balancing according to continuously 
changing workload conditions. Moreover, integrating Generative AI with real-time 

Page 22 of 24
Cortés Discover Networks            (2026) 2:33 
telemetry and edge analytics may facilitate intelligent energy-aware orchestration strate­
gies [18] that improve sustainability, reduce operational costs, and enhance resilience in 
next-generation AI-driven data centers.
Consequently, future investigations should explore hybrid architectures combining 
Transformer models, CNN-based spatial analysis, and generative simulation frame­
works to develop scalable, predictive, and autonomous cooling-management platforms 
for emerging AI, mobile, and IoT infrastructures.
5  Conclusion
Data centers are facing unprecedented changes as they require greater thermal den­
sity, adoption of neural networks, and higher demands for efficiency and resilience. 
The accelerated deployment of Artificial Intelligence (AI) workloads is redefining ther­
mal and energy requirements in modern data centers. The rapid increase in rack den­
sity—from traditional 5–10  kW per rack to 30–100  kW per rack—demonstrates that 
conventional air-based cooling architectures are no longer sustainable for high-perfor­
mance and AI-driven environments. This study confirms that rack-level liquid cooling, 
including immersion cooling and direct-to-chip approaches, provides a scalable, ther­
modynamically efficient alternative that maintains operational stability under extreme 
thermal loads. This interpretation is further supported by the variable importance analy­
sis in Table 6. Thermal and cooling-related variables include ΔT, Airflow, and Mass Flow. 
These variables consistently achieve the highest normalized importance. Their impor­
tance can reach up to 100% across all evaluated models. This result indicates that system 
performance is primarily governed by thermodynamic and fluid-dynamic mechanisms 
related to heat dissipation. The continued dominance of these variables across differ­
ent hidden-layer configurations shows the model is robust and generalizes well. These 
findings together provide strong empirical evidence. They confirm that effective thermal 
management drives stable system operation under high thermal loads.
Furthermore, integrating neural networks via a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) and 
Radial Basis Function (RBF) models, as implemented in other work [11–13], enables 
advanced analysis of key cooling metrics, enabling predictive modeling of energy con­
sumption and thermal behavior. The proposed Neural Networks-based framework dem­
onstrates that intelligent data-driven optimization can significantly enhance cooling 
efficiency, reduce energy waste, and support higher rack densities without compromis­
ing reliability. These findings position liquid cooling combined with AI-driven modeling 
as a strategic pillar for next-generation sustainable data center design.
Subsequent research should prioritize the development of real-time adaptive control 
systems that incorporate neural network predictions within data center cooling manage­
ment platforms. Expanding datasets to encompass hybrid cooling architectures, such as 
liquid-to-air and liquid-to-liquid systems, across diverse climatic regions would enhance 
model generalization and robustness.
Furthermore, investigating advanced neural network architectures, including convo­
lutional and transformer-based models, may improve predictive accuracy under highly 
dynamic AI workloads. Assessing the economic and lifecycle implications of large-scale 
adoption of liquid cooling, including capital expenditure (CAPEX), operational expen­
diture (OPEX), and sustainability metrics such as Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), 
remains essential.

Page 23 of 24
Cortés Discover Networks            (2026) 2:33 
The use of synthetic datasets combined with simulation-driven neural-network analy­
sis demonstrates a scalable methodology for evaluating thermal-management strate­
gies in emerging AI-oriented infrastructures. This approach not only enables controlled 
experimentation under diverse operational conditions but also establishes a foundation 
for future integration with Generative AI frameworks capable of producing realistic 
thermal-performance scenarios for autonomous optimization and predictive infrastruc­
ture management.
Finally, future studies should examine the interplay between cooling optimization and 
workload orchestration to facilitate a fully intelligent data center ecosystem, wherein AI 
systems both generate computational demand and autonomously optimize their thermal 
and energy footprints.

LC-Opt: Benchmarking Reinforcement Learning and 
Agentic AI for End-to-End Liquid Cooling 
Optimization in Data Centers 
 
 
 
Avisek Naug1†, Antonio Guillen1†, Vineet Kumar2, Scott Greenwood2, Wesley Brewer2, 
Sahand Ghorbanpour1, Ashwin Ramesh Babu1, Vineet Gundecha1, 
Ricardo Luna Gutierrez1, Soumyendu Sarkar1†∗ 
1Hewlett Packard Enterprise, 2Oak Ridge National Laboratory 
{avisek.naug, antonio.guillen, sahand.ghorbanpour, ashwin.ramesh-babu, 
vineet.gundecha, rluna, soumyendu.sarkar}@hpe.com 
{kumarv, greenwoodms, brewerwh}@ornl.gov 
 
Abstract 
Liquid cooling is critical for thermal management in high-density data centers with 
the rising AI workloads. However, machine learning-based controllers are essential 
to unlock greater energy efficiency and reliability, promoting sustainability. We 
present LC-Opt, a Sustainable Liquid Cooling (LC) benchmark environment, for 
reinforcement learning (RL) control strategies in energy-efficient liquid cooling 
of high-performance computing (HPC) systems. Built on the baseline of a high- 
fidelity digital twin of Oak Ridge National Lab’s Frontier Supercomputer cooling 
system, LC-Opt provides detailed Modelica-based end-to-end models spanning 
site-level cooling towers to data center cabinets and server blade groups. RL 
agents optimize critical thermal controls like liquid supply temperature, flow rate, 
and granular valve actuation at the IT cabinet level, as well as cooling tower (CT) 
setpoints through a Gymnasium interface, with dynamic changes in workloads. This 
environment creates a multi-objective real-time optimization challenge balancing 
local thermal regulation and global energy efficiency, and also supports additional 
components like a heat recovery unit (HRU). We benchmark centralized and 
decentralized multi-agent RL approaches, demonstrate policy distillation into 
decision and regression trees for interpretable control, and explore LLM-based 
methods that explain control actions in natural language through an agentic mesh 
architecture designed to foster user trust and simplify system management. LC-Opt 
democratizes access to detailed, customizable liquid cooling models, enabling the 
ML community, operators, and vendors to develop sustainable data center liquid 
cooling control solutions. 
 
 
1 Introduction 
The rapid growth of data-intensive applications in artificial intelligence (AI), high-performance 
computing (HPC), and cloud services has driven a sharp rise in data center energy demand. With 
increasing server power density, traditional air cooling has become both thermally and economically 
inadequate [1], particularly for modern CPUs [2] and GPUs [3]. This shift has accelerated the 
adoption of liquid cooling (LC), which offers higher heat removal efficiency and can cut cooling

39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025) Track on Datasets and Benchmarks. 

2 
 
 
Figure 1: System Overview of end-to-end Control of Liquid Cooled Data Center. The CDU RL agents control 
the HPC server cabinets. The Cooling Towers are controlled by the CT RL agents. 
 
energy and carbon footprint by up to 63% [4]. However, LC systems largely rely on static or 
rule-based controls [5, 6, 7], limiting their energy-saving potential. 
Optimizing LC in HPC data centers is complex due to tight coupling with HVAC subsystems—CDUs, 
heat exchangers (HX), cooling towers (CT), and pumps [8, 9, 10]. Designing dynamic rule-based 
strategies for such systems is impractical. While Deep RL has shown promise in domains like 
robotics and HVAC, its application to large-scale LC systems is constrained by the absence of realistic 
testbeds. To address this, we introduce LC-Opt, a benchmarking framework extending Oak Ridge 
National Lab’s (ORNL) high-fidelity Modelica Digital Twin (DT) of the Frontier supercomputer [11] 
with RL-ready control interfaces. Code, licenses, and setup instructions for LC-Opt are available at 
GitHub2. The main contributions of this work are: 
1. Liquid Cooling Control Benchmark: Evaluate control strategies for an HPC data center with 
ORNL’s Frontier supercomputer’s digital twin as baseline and additional features. 
2. End-to-end Customizable and Scalable Benchmark: Supports energy optimization of fine- 
grained Blade-Group (BG) server temperature control, cooling tower (CT), and heat reuse (HRU). 
3. Gymnasium interface: Supports RL, LLM-based, and traditional controllers (ASHRAE G36 
[12]) for real-time control strategies. 
4. Multi-agent Control: Supports single-agent, multi-agent, homogeneous, and hybrid RL policies 
in customizable data center setups. 
5. Granular & Hybrid Control: CDU control agents regulate HPC cabinet temperatures by adjust- 
ing inlet temperature setpoints, pump flow rates, and blade-group valve openings. Cooling 
Tower control agents minimize energy consumption by modulating return water temperatures. 
6. Ablation and scalability: Reference evaluation of agents and scalability for large-scale cooling 
systems, and hybrid policy effectiveness for blade-level cooling control and cooling tower. 
7. Policy interpretability: Supports model distillation [13] for policy extraction with LLM and 
decision tree-based strategies, aiding researchers and operators with policy validation. 
8. LLM explainability and Agentic Design: Supports LLM controllers that generate natural lan- 
guage explanations of control actions to enhance operator trust and simplify system management. 
 
2 Related Work 
The growing energy demands of data centers and their increasing impact on global carbon emissions 
have driven research to improve cooling systems. Traditional cooling methods, such as static setpoints 
and basic rule-based controllers [14, 15], have been widely used in the past. Although these methods 
helped ensure stable temperatures, they were not efficient enough to handle modern data centers’ 
complex and changing conditions. Liquid cooling (LC) has become an efficient alternative to air 
cooling due to its ability to transfer heat more efficiently and handle larger workloads [16, 17]. 
However, managing LC systems is challenging due to the need to control many factors, such as flow

3 
 
 
 
 
Blade Group 2 
 
 
 
Figure 2: Frontier’s Cooling System [11] 
 
rates, temperatures, and valve settings [18]. Traditional methods often fail to fully optimize these 
systems, especially when workloads exhibit severely skewed allocation across clusters. Machine 
learning (ML) methods have been increasingly applied for predictive thermal management [19, 20] 
and control [21, 22], using historical and current data to perform fine-tuned cooling. While RL has 
been effective in optimizing air-cooled data centers, its application in LC systems is still emerging. 
[11] presents a framework demonstrating modeling of transient thermo-fluidic dynamics and energy 
efficiency for liquid-cooled exascale supercomputers, in Modelica. This work significantly extends 
the Modelica model with a fine-grained AI enabled control interfaces wrapping it in a Gymnasium- 
compatible framework, enabling scalable RL and generative AI-based control for high-fidelity, 
energy-efficient cooling—advancing beyond static rules like ASHRAE Guideline 36 [12]. 
 
3 LC-Opt Description 
First, in Section 3.1, we provide a high-level 
 
description of the Frontier Liquid Cooling sys- 
tem and how we have augmented the com- 
pute block with blade-level cooling, coolant set- 
point and flow rate control, and Cooling Tower 
water setpoint control. This enables machine 
learning-based temperature and power manage- 
ment. Then we provide the implementation de- 
tails of the modeling (Section 3.2) and control 
problems (Section 3.3) included in LC-Opt. 
 
Frontier Cabinet 
 
Figure 3: Blade Level Cooling control is one of the 
Modelica modeling augmentations to the Frontier Liquid 
Cooling system model. 
3.1 Frontier Liquid Cooling System for Machine Learning Applications 
Figure 2 illustrates the Frontier Liquid Cooling (LC) system. On the right, there are arrays of cabinets 
that house servers (in racks), grouped into blades. Each cabinet is paired with a Cooling Distribution 
Unit (CDU-Rack Loop), which extracts heat via a heat exchanger(HX) and pumps by adjusting 
coolant temperature and flow rate. Frontier includes 25 such CDU-Rack pairs, transferring heat to a 
central Hot Water System (HTW, center of figure). This heat is ultimately rejected to the environment 
via the Cooling Tower (CT) Loop, which employs fans for forced-draft cooling through sensible and 
latent processes (Cooling Tower Loop in the figure). CT power consumption depends on wetbulb 
temperature, supply temperature setpoint, and incoming thermal load. The system also features a 
Heat Recovery Unit (HRU), an intermediate heat exchanger that reuses server waste heat for ancillary 
heating (e.g., residential or district applications). 
The original Modelica model employed ASHRAE-based or static rule-based controllers [12]. We 
augmented the model to support RL-based control to enhance temperature regulation at CDUs and 
optimize energy use at CTs. The most elaborate augmentation is the blade group (BG) control for 
each cabinet, as shown in Figure 3. A blade group is a collection of servers that are served by one 
branch of the cooling liquid. For the Cooling Tower, traditional staging and return temperature 
controls were replaced with RL-based supervisory control(Cooling Tower ML Control). Similarly, 
for CDU-cabinet pairs, RL agents now regulate coolant temperature setpoints, flow rates (CDU ML 
Controls). These two augmentations are further shown in Figure 11 in Appendix C for advanced 
Modelica users. 

4 
 
 
 
Figure 4: Functional Design of LC-Opt. 1) AutoCSM API to create a Modelica model for a Data Center 
Cooling system based on the System Description in JSON format. 2) Hierarchical structure of the cooling 
system model. 3) LC-Opt Gymnasium environment provides the Python interface for the Modelica Functional 
Mockup Unit (FMU) binary executable. 4) MDPs for multi-agent RL cooling control. 
3.2 LC-Opt Modeling 
The model implementations in LC-Opt are based on the liquid cooling (LC) system description 
provided in Section 3.1. Parts 1, 2, and 3 in figure 4 comprise the modeling process. 
1. We first specify the composition of the LC system in a JSON file in a hierarchical manner. This 
allows us to build customizable LC setups that include individual cabinets, the cooling distribution 
units (CDU), the heat exchangers for intermediate as well as heat reuse primary and secondary 
loops, valves, pumps, sensors, and finally, the cooling tower. It further allows us to specify 
components that define the nature of control, whether rule-based or RL-enabled, the data sources 
to be used as exogenous variables, the system parameterization, etc. The components of the LC 
system specified in the JSON file are then read using the AutoCSM API [23], and it creates a 
Modelica model of the data center liquid cooling system 
2. The system’s hierarchical specification enables the creation of complex yet interpretable LC 
architectures. Advanced users can visualize and modify system details via Modelica IDEs (e.g., 
Dymola, OpenModelica), using components from the datacenterCoolingModel library [10]. LC- 
Opt uniquely supports blade-group (BG) valve control, allowing fine-grained actuation based on 
heat input to the blade groups. To our knowledge, this is the first framework offering detailed 
modeling and benchmarking of hybrid control, serving both ML researchers (e.g., multihead 
policies) and data center practitioners. 
3. To enable ML-based control of the LC system, we exported the Modelica model to a Functional 
Mockup Unit (FMU) using a Modelica compiler. The FMU, a non-linear state-space system, 
integrates with Python frameworks like Gymnasium [24]. It accepts both exogenous and control 
inputs, updates its internal state, and produces outputs for downstream use. Python interfaces to 
the FMU are standardized via FMPy [25] and PyFMI [26]. Exogenous variables simulate non- 
control dynamics such as heat generation at blade groups or external weather, influencing system 
behavior like cooling tower performance. It supports various FMUs to test custom environments 
and evaluate RL scalability, particularly for hybrid action spaces in HPC. A detailed guide for 
compiling custom LC-Opt environments is included in the Supplemental and GitHub Readme. 
 
3.3 LC-Opt Control 
4. To facilitate control applications for the LC system, LC-Opt wraps the FMU with the Gymasium 
interface. We primarily focus on two problems for LC-Opt. Firstly, at the higher level, we wish to 
reduce the overall data center energy cooling consumption, which is dominated by the CTs. Hence, 
we build a CT Markov Decision Process (MDP) as shown in Figure 4. The detailed formulation of 
the MDP is shown further in Table 1. The other goal is to ensure optimum operating temperatures 
of the blade groups. Hence, we create the Blade Group Level MDP that focuses on this aspect of 
the problem. Details of the corresponding MDP are provided in Table 2. 
A key aspect of LC-Opt is that both MDPs share the same FMU transition model (T ), enabling mutual 
influence. However, due to weak thermal coupling (Figure 2) and sheer state space size, single-agent 
or centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) for multiagents was ineffective and

This is due to the large state space and Frontier’s scale (∼ 104 blade groups). To address this, we test 
a centralized inference per MDP during rollout, as detailed later. 
 
4 RL applications on LC-Opt 
4.1 Centralized Action Execution in Multiagent RL 
As discussed in Section 3.3, the environment supports diverse RL formulations, including multi-agent 
strategies, where they independently control the Cooling Tower (CT) and Blade Group (BG) MDPs 
(Tables 1 and 2). However, standard multi-agent setups face scalability issues as the number of CTs 
and BGs increases, due to growing state-action spaces. To mitigate this, we implement a centralized 
action (CA) approach with state-action decomposition, leveraging behavioral similarity across CTs 
and BGs. This approach is detailed in Figure 5 for CDU and Blade Group CA RL and in Figure 
12 in the Appendix. for Cooling Tower CA RL. The BG MDP observation is decomposed per 
blade group. While BGs within a cabinet are interdependent due to fan dynamics and workload 
allocation, BGs across cabinets are conditionally independent [27]. For the CT MDP, we partition 
the observation space per tower, enabling batch inference across towers. Since CT operations are 
loosely coupled, primarily through shared power consumption, we treat CT power as a blocking 
d-separation (directional separation) [27] variable. However, return water temperature remains 
partially coupled across towers. To account for this, we include all return temperatures in each 
decomposed observation. Wet bulb temperature is also retained to capture humidity constraints on 
cooling capacity. For each MDP, batched inference enables parallel rollout and value estimation. To 
prevent experience contamination across parallel batches, we allocate separate rollout buffers per CT 
and cabinet, avoiding data overlap. While this batching improves inference efficiency, it introduces a 
limitation in terms of the memory cost, proportional to the data center’s scale.

where the first head generates the scaled temperature setpoint and flow rate in the [−1, 1] range using

5 LLM-LC: An Agentic-AI Platform for Real Time Operation of Liquid 
Cooled Data Centers 
To address the complex, multi-objective challenge of optimizing liquid cooling in High-Performance 
Computing (HPC) data centers, we introduce an Agentic LLM-based Digital Twin architecture. 
Interpretable and explainable LLM controller fine-tuned using distillation from trained RL policies 
serve as the basis for the framework. It moves beyond monolithic, "black-box" controllers by 
decomposing the control problem into a collaborative ecosystem of specialized, LLM-powered 
agents. 
 
5.1 Policy Distillation of the Trained RL Agents in to LLMs and Decision Trees for 
explainability 
Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) agents have shown strong performance in sequential decision- 
making, but their lack of interpretability limits deployment in safety-critical domains such as data 
centers. We hence show, how LLMs can be fine-tuned to perform interpretable control and generate 
explainable policies. This is primarily achieved by distilling where trained RL policy Experience 
Data is used to fine-tune the performance of an Instruction-tuned LLM as shown in Figure 6. [28] 
We employ Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT), 
specifically the QLoRA method, to efficiently adapt the 
LLM to mimic the oracle’s decision-making process [29]. 
The resulting fine-tuned LLM not only functions as a con- 
troller but can also provide natural language explanations 
for its actions, bridging the gap between the high perfor- 
mance of RL policies and the need for transparency in 
critical applications. As an alternative, Decision Trees 
(DTs) also offer interpretable policies and are used to dis- 
till RL policies as part of ablation in our results. The 
process to generate the Experience Data in Figure 6 is 
discussed in details in the Appendix A 
 
5.2 Multi-Agent System for Explainable Control 
Figure 6: Policy Distillation in to LLMs 
from trained RL policy 
As illustrated in Figure 7, the agents communicate over a central message bus to achieve a control 
system that is not only high-performing but also inherently transparent, resilient, and explainable. 
Our architecture is composed of several distinct classes of agents and tools, each responsible for a 
specific aspect of the control and monitoring process. 
• Reasoning & Decision Agents: At the heart of the system is the Control Agent, a reasoning 
engine responsible for generating real-time control actions. This agent’s policy is fine-tuned using 
deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) on a high-fidelity digital twin of the cooling system. It processes 
system states and leverages an LLM guided control model to make decisions. It is complemented 
by a Sensor Agent, which serves as the system’s interface to the digital twin, monitoring system 
states, performing necessary data preprocessing, and transmitting the Control Agent’s actions to 
the actuators. 
• Maintenance Agents: To ensure long-term robustness and system health, a suite of maintenance 
agents operates continuously. The Agent Monitor performs meta-level oversight, tracking the 
performance and resource utilization of the other agents and recommending optimization strategies. 
The Maintenance Agent focuses on the physical system’s integrity, monitoring health metrics, 
identifying anomalies and trends in thermal dynamics, predicting potential failures, and prescribing 
preventative maintenance actions. 
• Planning & Interface Agents: High-level strategic management is handled by the Configuration 
Agent, which manages system configurations such as scaling, control parameters, and the hyper- 
parameters of the LLM agents. Crucially for human-in-the-loop interaction and trust, the User 
Interface Agent provides deep system transparency. Its Visualization component offers natural

• Trust Agents and Tools: The entire system is coordinated by an Orchestration Agent, which
